speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEFICIENCY PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that the agricultural stabilization board has been authorized to continue to stabilize the price of hogs to producers for the calendar year 1964 by means of a deficiency payment program. The board is authorized to pay hog producers the amount by which the prescribed price of $23.65 per hundredweight exceeds the price determined by the board to be the national average price at which grade A hogs are sold by the producers during 1964.
As in recent years, the board will determine at the end of the year the national average price to producers at which grade A hogs were sold. If this average price should be less than the prescribed support price of $23.65 per hundredweight, then the difference will be paid as a deficiency payment to each registered hog producer on a maximum of 100 hogs graded A or B under federal inspection.
In 1963 the national average price received by producers for grade A hogs was $27.30 per hundredweight, which is well above the $23.65 support price. Therefore no deficiency payment is being made for the 1963 calendar year. The outlook for hog prices for 1964 is reasonably favourable, and prices should not fall much below the high level of 1963.

I appreciate the opportunity of repeating our policy in respect of the national parks of Canada. We are restricted to maintaining our national parks in a state of nature, which means the preservation of the wilderness aspect of the parks. This will continue. I knew I had time at my disposal, but I was not altogether sure whether the question period was over or not.

Mr. Speaker, last night, when the house adjourned, I was reading an article which appeared in L'Action, entitled:
The consumer is king.
The article ends this way:
The consumer's interest is essentially the legitimate interest of the salesman, the manufacturer and the public services: the consumer's interest is the general interest. The consumer is king in our modern economy. We should not forget that.
Mr. Speaker, very often, we seem to leave out the consumers' needs. And, in a country such as ours, it is quite essential to take these needs into consideration, because the day a government disregards them, we might as well say that such a government does not care about the Canadian people.

As I was saying yesterday, there has been a great deal of activity in this country in an effort for national unity, in an attempt to co-ordinate all the efforts of both nations in this country to form one strong nation, the Canadian nation. But there cannot be peace while there is one section of the country which is under the impression that it is not making economic progress and is not receiving its just share from confederation.
I would remind hon. members of the points I enumerated yesterday concerning industry in eastern Canada, particularly in Quebec, and concerning unemployment in that province. I called attention also to certain taxes which are imposed all over Canada; provincial taxes, federal income taxes, municipal taxes, school board taxes and so on. From this it can be seen that consumers, the Canadian people, are saturated with these taxes and cannot absorb any more.
Our tax system at the present time is driving the people to bankruptcy. Add these things together and you have a total loss of 25 years of progress in the province of Quebec. We do not blame the Anglo-Saxons or the English part of Canada. That is not the view of the province. What the province wants now is the restoration of its right to a full share from the federal administration. The province would like to have more control over its currency, more control over its direct and indirect taxation, so that it might take the reins itself and achieve its
294	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Langlois own economic progress. It does not wish to do this at the expense of the other provinces. Until Quebec is given these possibilities there is bound to be friction between English Canadians and French Canadians, not because of differences in race or language but because there is an economic problem at the bottom of it all. French Canada wishes only to be an equal partner in confederation, nothing more. That was the basis of confederation in Canada.
We do not expect to make French Canadians out of English Canadians in Canada, nor do I see French Canadians becoming English Canadians, either. What I see are two Canadian nations on an equal basis striving for national unity and for the good of Canada as a whole. We must secure economic progress in both nations. In the past 96 years the country has been administered from this parliament by both Conservative and Liberal governments. What has this brought Canada in a hundred years? What has Canada received from it. The story economically speaking, has been friction upon friction, injustice upon injustice. Then one day we wake up and say "How is it that Canada is not satisfied with confederation?" I think the basis of our difficulty lies in the fact that Canada, by reason of its present monetary policies, cannot solve its economic problems. There must be a radical change in our economic system if these problems are to be solved.
As I mentioned yesterday, we have in Canada natural resources of all kinds. We have technicians and we have engineers, yet there is unemployment across the country. Why are we suffering from economic stagnation at the moment, in the face of such a situation? One could understand stagnation if there were nothing to be developed, or if there were a lack of labour or of technicians. But at the present time the only thing which is causing economic stagnation is the fact that the Canadian government is telling all the ten provinces that there is no money available for the development of our country. It is a fight between the provinces and the federal government to see which is to have the greatest share of tax revenues.
The Canadian people are saturated with taxes. It is not possible to collect from them more than they possess. We need to change this situation and amend the Bank of Canada Act so the federal government can obtain credit, interest free, for the development of public services. Until we have that we will continue to crawl; we will continue on our hands and knees in front of foreign moneylenders either from the United States or Europe; we will continue to be backbenchers as far as economics are concerned. We must

have control of our own credit so that when we ultimately develop our natural resources Canada will, in the final analysis, still belong to Canadians.
We have among English speaking and French speaking Canadians all the good will that is needed to assure the co-operation necessary to solve this problem. National unity will not be realized until we have such an understanding between our two great nations. We have that understanding in this house. 1 am sure every member of this house wants national unity. Nobody wants to leave English Canada aside, and nobody wants to leave French Canada aside. But we have to understand the basic problem first. Everyone is striving and working to attain this national unity so we can finally have a stronger, truer Canada as a whole.
In the last resort the action to be taken falls upon the present government. We in the opposition can say all we like; all Canadians with good will across the country can say what they wish. In the final analysis the course must be taken by the government and the responsibility falls upon them. It is up to them now to find a solution. They have had the problem placed before them for the past few months, and Canada's future is in their hands.
Let us hope, Mr. Speaker, that the solution to this problem will be a fair one to all Canadians. With the good will of the Canadian people, with the help of every member of this house, the government should be taking action now. We cannot save confederation until the Prime Minister and his ministers accept the responsibility and have the desire to save confederation. The decision as to the final course to follow and the final solution to this problem is the Prime Minister's alone. It is his decision as to what alternative should be taken and when to take it. The finai decision lies between you alone, the Prime Minister, and God. You choose it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the pattern set by previous speakers, my first words will be to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne; furthermore, I cannot let this occasion pass without congratulating the new ministers and those who have assumed new functions.
Allow me, however, to say how pleased I am by the appointment of the new Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) who will be responsible eventually and very soon, I hope, for rural development. I am particularly happy for the simple reason that I can now expect that rural development will at last come to the fore, and that this is an effort to find solutions to the crucial problems facing eastern farmers and, in particular, those of Bellechasse who make up more than 70 per cent of the population in my riding.
Mr. Speaker, allow me at the beginning to make a few remarks about the very precarious situation in which live, or rather try to live, the majority of my fellow citizens of Bellechasse. My hon. colleague, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Beer), was able to see the situation for himself last summer when he accepted my invitation to visit the farmers in my riding. The hon. member was able to see the poverty and misery which are the lot of most of our farmers, especially in the southern part, the most hilly in the riding. Believe it or not, the income of most farmers in Bellechasse is less than $1,000 a year, in a country as prosperous as ours, and that in spite of their putting in a work week which is far from the 40 or 45-hour week, since they work twice that many hours and even more. They work hard, in very difficult conditions, and they get very little out of it.
I therefore want to say to the house, on behalf of all farmers of my riding, that I am aware of the hardship they are undergoing, which I have shared, because I was brought up on a low income farm. I want to tell those people how much I admire their indomitable courage and their persistent labour, the like of which is rarely seen today. I also want to tell them that I can understand their discontent with regard to the various governments.
Believe me, Mr. Speaker, those fine artisans have really grounds for complaining, because very little has been done for them until now. They have been somehow forgotten and their existence ignored. I am telling this true fact, even as a member on the government side, because it is, indeed, a fact, as they have been neglected long enough. I also want them to know that their problems are my first concern, and that I spare no constructive 20220-20i
The Address-Mr. Laverdiere effort which might help them. And I repeat "constructive effort", because, in my humble opinion, mere lamentations will hardly bring about the realistic and concrete solutions that are needed.
I do not think that repeating, shouting from the rooftops that our farmers cannot make both ends meet will help them. I rather believe in a sensible organization which will bring about a positive solution. I know how complex the position of the eastern farmers is. Yet, I cannot but repeat that I deplore that so little action in this field has been taken until now. There is, of course, the feed grain storage which was paid by the government this year. The storage is adequate, as well as the shipping grants for this grain. I fully appreciate those measures.
Nevertheless, I wish we could go further and more quickly ahead in this field, and that an organization responsible for the required control of grain purchases and sales be set up as soon as possible for our eastern farmers, in order to put an end to speculation at their expense.
Some brokers have made millions in these transactions, but that was not enough. In the last few years they have attempted to control not only the buying and selling of grain, but even cattle breeding, by financing some farmers' projects in that field. Is it out of altruism? Is it to save the family farm, as they are trying to tell us, that these brokers show such an interest in breeding and grain? It is rather easy to doubt that apparent intention when some of those very companies got rich at the expense of the eastern farmers and furthermore, when they are directly interested in the sale of farm products. I admit that this way we allow certain farmers to make a profit, but that profit would certainly be considerably increased, at least doubled, if it were not for that trust which controls grain transactions from western Canada or the United States and also the marketing of farm products.
I am positive, Mr. Speaker, that a detailed investigation would show control allowing some companies to make an unreasonable profit which private enterprise is not permitted.

speechtext:
I am sorry but I still have some remarks to make. However, if I have any time left, I shall be pleased to answer the hon. member.
I should also like to mention the increasing harm that is done to bona fide farmers, I mean those whose main occupation is farming, by men of all professions who raise cattle today. A number of professionals, whose profession is most profitable, go in for that sideline, and so take on the market a place which, in my opinion, should be left to farmers. Farming is one of the most noble trades. Let every man stick to his trade. The farming profession is entitled to the same protection as the others.
As the Prime Minister said to the house last Thursday:
No field of activity is more important for our country than agriculture and forests.
And a little farther he went on:
A number of the most acute problems resulting from low farm income arise especially in eastern Canada.
I will add that certain farmers must be unusually courageous and love tilling the soil -something, unfortunately, which is disappearing-to hold on to their farm, while waiting patiently for assistance that is slow to come. However, in view of the present situation, many who struggled year in year out for a means of livelihood, who tried to stay despite all the difficulties, now find themselves compelled, though reluctantly, to leave their farm.
Then skilled agricultural workers, experts in the true sense of the word, though quite often having no other trade, are deserting the country in great numbers for the city, where they become the first ones to be stricken by unemployment, especially nowadays where skilled labour is required in most jobs offered by industry.
Steps must be taken so that the farmers' income may reach at least the average level for other trades.
Too often our farmers' income cover only the incurred expenses; not being sure to get adequate and stable prices for their products and moreover suspecting, with reason, that they are being abused somewhere along the line, they get discouraged, and not without cause. Nevertheless, the family farm is and will continue to be the most fundamental enterprise in our society, and it is our duty to protect it.
I should also like to make a few remarks concerning industry. It is not my intention to speak at length about it, although I think that new industries must be set up in Bellechasse to absorb the labour available in that area. A few industries are maintained there whose development is due to the acumen and ability

of their management; but other industries are much more needed now than they were in 1956, when the then hon. member for Bellechasse Mr. Ovide Laflamme, described these needs in the speech he delivered as seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne; Mr. Laflamme stated then the following:
Each year, however, many of Bellechasse's native sons have to look elsewhere for jobs. That is a problem which could be solved, at least in part, by the development of small scale industry. These young people leave our constituency for larger centres where, especially in winter, they merely swell the ranks of the unemployed. I feel that government assistance to small industries would go a long way towards solving the difficult problem of unemployment as well as the housing shortage.
I would add that the movement has gained momentum these past few years not only among the young people, but also among entire families; they would have liked to remain in their native parishes, but they had to move to the cities because of the lack of work.
The industrial development bank helps the small industry by granting loans, but I feel that this government agency could lighten the burden of the small industry by reducing its rate of interest and by easing its lending formalities, especially in the case of small industries.
It should be noted that the large industries feel the need to rely on smaller companies to which they may award subcontracts. They are sure to make savings that way and the automobile industry is an example of that. In co-operation with the provinces, the federal government has set up a program of financial assistance to the small industry.
In addition, the tendency is towards the decentralization of industry. Administration and technical courses are being given and, in my opinion, those courses should be more readily available to everybody, especially to people who live in rural districts. I also feel that the government should strive to establish new industries in strategic areas, also called depressed areas, and insist more than it does on the decentralization of industry in the best interest of those areas.
In that connection, I must say that I am disappointed because only a few parishes in my riding are considered as designated areas. Those areas have been selected on the basis of statistics supplied by national employment offices. I admit that statistics show some facts, but they do not show everything. It is not necessary to make a thorough investigation in order to realize that Bellechasse, for instance, is one of the poorest areas in the province of Quebec and that personal income there is extremely low.

Mr. Speaker, we provide millions of dollars in assistance to underdeveloped countries and, believe me, I am not against that. It is my duty to point out, however, that there are, right here in Canada, areas that are in even greater need of such assistance than some foreign countries to which we give millions.
I admit that these underdeveloped countries need some assistance and we are justified in helping them. Agronomists, technicians, all types of professionals are sent to these countries at the expense of the Canadian government. However, our farmers here can hardly reach a district agronomist who is swamped with paper work and is unable to deal with farmers. Yet, farmers feel that they need some guidance and advice; they are anxious to learn and improve their lot and it must be recognized that, in agriculture, the basic problem is education and guidance.
Mr. Speaker, before making a few remarks on national unity, I wish to mention that I agree entirely with the views set forth a few days ago by my colleague for Bonaventure (Mr. Bechard) about the kind of programs broadcast by the C.B.C. for the Canadian people.
As the hon. member said, surely it is not with all those scenes of gangsterism, crime, passion and immorality now taking up most of the time on television, surely it is not with those meaningless plays which take an hour and a half to say things that could be told in five minutes, plays that are called modern out of snobbery, surely, it is not with this kind of programming that we are going to raise the intellectual and moral level of the Canadian people.
And to show you that the population of my constituency is anxious to see an improvement in televised broadcasts, I received complaints against a television program put on last Tuesday evening.
May I say that people want entertainment on television, but decent entertainment where butchery and scenes of violence and passion have no place.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make on Canada's main topic of discussion at the present time, that is to say national unity.
I am aware, like every one else in Quebec, of all those ideas of independence rising in all circles across "la belle province". During the last few years especially, it would seem that French Canadians have been trying to make up for lost time and their nationalism is finding many ways of expression.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that the nationalist unrest in Quebec is not a passing fancy. On the contrary, it satisfies a deeply
The Address-Mr. Laverdiere felt desire that circumstances had only repressed. Until now, French Canadians had resigned themselves to a situation which history had somewhat imposed upon them.
Yet, he knows today that this situation is not normal and that we cannot any longer accept to be considered as foreigners in our own country. We ask our partners in confederation to try to understand that exultation because of our freedom regained and the awakening of the deepest and noblest aspirations of the French Canadian soul. We ask them to start a true dialogue which will pave the way to a deep and realistic mutual understanding.
I am most happy to proclaim my feelings of pride in seeing that the vitality and nationalism of a youthful people is openly expressed and I can only subscribe to the efforts of our young people who want Quebec to develop as soon as possible and become an adult nation.
However, I deplore the manifestations of extremists, who will not add anything constructive to this irreversible struggle which we have undertaken in order to become equal partners in confederation. I deplore also the unfortunate and unfounded statements which can only be due to petty politics. Common sense and reason certainly remain the best weapons at our disposal.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that there is a superior race. There are races, each with its own language, its culture, its customs, its traditions, its qualities, its deficiencies. Let us learn to know each other as we are, and we shall get along.

As an example, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I have great admiration and respect for my mother tongue, but this does not mean I consider it superior to the English language. Each is a great language, but each in its own capacity. I have had the opportunity of knowing English speaking Canadians, especially when I taught at the Academie Proven-cher in St. Boniface and also while I followed courses given at the University of Western Ontario. I am sure that by taking time out to look around, and thus trying to become better acquainted, we will realize just how fond we would be of one another, and we would then me most willing and proud to join as a united family from the Atlantic to the Pacific.

Before I conclude my remarks, may I add, for the guidance of my fellow citizens whose ethnic origin is not the same as mine, that I think this surge of nationalism should be a motive of pride and hope for all Canadians. It seems to me that those fellow citizens could

The Address-Mr. MacEwan have only one conceivable reason, if any, to consider us as inferiors, and that would be the lack in us, French Canadians, of pride, and of nationalism.
Therefore, I say to them: "Rejoice with us, since your partners are proud of what they are, proud of their culture, proud of their origin, proud of their language and traditions. They are partners who can stand up and fight with all their vitality, their youth, their vigour, to make Canada, our country, the most united, the most prosperous country in the world.

Mr. Speaker, may I first join with others who have taken part in this debate in congratulating the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. In doing so I do not necessarily intend to indicate that I agree with the substance of what they said, but the form in which they carried out their duties was excellent.
I should like, however, to take exception to some of the remarks made by the seconder, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. I am not going into detail in my reply, but I should like to refer to some of the remarks the hon. member made when he offered some advice to the Prime Minister and his government as well as to the Leader of the Opposition. He referred to the speech from the throne as a lean, progressive, businesslike document. He characterized it as a let us get on with the job type of speech. The government, he said, had indicated its willingness and its desire to give to the people of Canada the things for which they are looking, and parliament should address itself to the problems of the country.
Then the hon. member said he realized that the Leader of the Opposition had certain important responsibilities; that it rested in his hands whether or not parliament is effective or grinds to a complete standstill. I stand subject to correction, but I believe the hon. member first entered this parliament at the last session. I do not believe he was a member when the party to which I belong formed the government and, shortly after presenting the speech from the throne, were thrown out of office. He was not here when obstruction was the theme of the hon. gentlemen opposite. Perhaps if he will wait a little longer he will be able to see just what goes on, and what a party in opposition can do.
If the hon. member thinks that obstruction may be carried out or was carried out at the last session, I should like to refer him to a witness who is definitely not for the defence on this side, namely the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill). During the last
[Mr. Laverdiere.l
session, on November 29, as recorded on page 5268 of Hansard, the minister referred to this subject of obstruction. He said:
Certainly I have not, and I want to make that very clear. I have not made any such allegation at any time about the opposition. I think there has been a reasonable measure of co-operation-
Then on the same page of Hansard the minister is reported as having said:
Perhaps the hon. gentleman will remember- and here perhaps I am breaking the rules myself by referring to the debate on redistribution the other day-that I am one of those who think there ought to be debate in parliament, and I do not regard debate as obstruction. I have not said and I have not thought that, taken by and large in this session of parliament, particularly since we met in September, there has been anything I would be inclined to describe as obstruction.
May I refer the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard to this statement; and may I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that debate is the essence of parliament. In so far as responsibility is concerned, I suggest that he recall what has happened in the last few days in so far as his ministers are concerned. The party to which I belong has shown it knows what responsibility means and will carry on the role of a responsible opposition party.
I do not want to forget the Minister of National Defence. I recall that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard appeared on a C.B.C. broadcast with him not long ago. However, since it is almost one o'clock, may I call it one o'clock before I launch into these few remarks?
At one o'clock the house took recess.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at one o'clock I was entering upon paragraph 2 of the speech which I had prepared, and I had referred to a program which I saw on a C.B.C. free time broadcast in which the two principle participants were the Minister of National Defence and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. During the broadcast the minister set forth various matters of importance in the field of national defence. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard can correct me if I am wrong, but I recall that when he was asked about the major cut-backs and the cancellation of the general purpose frigate program he said he believed the constituents of his area on the west coast would go along with these decisions as being necessary.
He, of course, is a member from the west coast, but the people on the east coast are not quite so happy. If I may I would like to

The Address-Mr. MacEwan '
refer to the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of January 9, 1964, where there is an article headed "Cut-back hits N.S. hardest." It states that:
The scrapping of three Tribal class destroyer escorts and ten minesweepers may eventually mean a manpower cut of up to 10 per cent.
On the page after that there is a photograph of the minesweeper H.M.C.S. Quinte, with a caption saying that it, along with her five sister ships in the first Canadian minesweeping squadron, will be placed in reserve in Halifax.
The reason I mention this is that no alternative program was proposed in place of the general purpose frigate program, and this leaves a gap in the matter of shipbuilding facilities. In the short period of time I have been in Ottawa I have had something to do with the navy and defence production. It is common knowledge that it takes a long period of time to put a ship construction program into effect, especially a naval shipbuilding program, and in this connection I would like to refer to the New Glasgow Evening News of January 28 last, which carried a report stating:
Many officials in the industry, in government and in the navy say they fear the shipyards will lose much of their skill and experience because of the delay in launching a new naval shipbuilding program in place of the cancelled super frigates.
Of course we are looking forward to the white paper which the minister has announced he will present next month.

speechtext:
When I have finished I shall be glad to let the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan) ask me questions. I shall refer to the Halifax area, but more particularly to the Pictou shipyard in my own constituency, because the smaller ships have been repaired in those yards. Destroyer escorts cannot be repaired there, but the ship I have referred to, H.M.C.S. Quinte, was repaired there last year. The effect of the government's decision means that the larger yards will now be vying for work with the smaller yards, and it also means there will be a lesser number of ships because of the cut-back. I submit this should not be carried out in a piecemeal way, but rather that it should be done in an organized manner, and an alternative program should have been presented before this cut-back was implemented.
In the broadcast to which I previously referred, shots were shown of the minister going back and forth between the ships of the Atlantic fleet. Of course those shots were taken when we had ships, last December.
They also showed him with army units. That, of course, was when the army had arms.
So that I may not pass over any of the services, perhaps I may be permitted to refer to another report which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, also in January last, though I regret I cannot give the exact date. This is a Canadian Press story under an Ottawa dateline, written by Dave McIntosh under the heading " 'Bus Driver' Role Forecast for R.C.A.F.". To be fair, the words are added-"But Anti-Sub Role Would Be Maintained". The article says:
The R.C.A.F. will be withdrawn from all its combat roles, with the possible exception of antisubmarine patrol work, within five years, authorities forecast Monday.
They predicted that the service will become an almost exclusively transport force and that its combat roles in home air defence and in nuclear bombing in Europe will be eliminated by 1969 or earlier.
Plans are already being made to expand the R.C.A.F. station at Trenton, Ontario, headquarters for transport command.
Referring to discontent in the forces, the article goes on to say:
Meanwhile, there is discontent in the armed forces about some reasons the government is giving for defence reductions.
Sources said the current economy drive in the defence department makes good sense but they feel the government shouldn't attach extraneous or irrelevant reasons to announcements concerning defence cuts. They cited these two examples from Friday's announcement of the disbandment of two Voodoo squadrons:
The announcement said planes from the disbanded squadrons at Ottawa and North Bay, Ontario would be moved to the squadrons at Chatham, N.B. and Bagotville, Quebec, "to improve operational efficiency and promote economy".
And this, I believe, is the important part:
Informed sources said there will be economy. But the decision flew in the face of established NORAD policy of dispersing interceptors as much as possible to try to avoid their total destruction on the ground with two or three long range missiles.
The announcement also said removal of the 10 Voodoos from Ottawa would reduce the density of air traffic at Uplands airport here. But the defence department had announced previously that the electronic warfare squadron at St. Hubert, Quebec, will be moved to Uplands. It has 18 CF-100 jets.
We look forward with interest to the white paper which the minister is to bring forward before too long. I know that this white paper, even though it may deal only with generalities, will receive the fullest scrutiny by members on this side of the house.
I should like to refer now to the subject of unemployment. Some people say this is no longer a national problem but a regional one. Well, they can have their own views on this, but I should like to refer to the situation in the Atlantic provinces, and particularly to unemployment in my own area. Suggestions

The Address-Mr. MacEwan have been made that the Atlantic development board, which was set up when the party to which I belong was in power, would look after things, since a fund of $100 million was to be at the disposal of that board. However, as has been pointed out by several previous speakers, including the hon. member for Cumberland and the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg, one single grant, namely $20 million to the Saint John river project in New Brunswick, will use up a large part of that amount. Even the present chairman of the board is not sure where additional funds will come from. Speaking at a meeting held, I think, in Ottawa in January, he said he did not know if there would be any further funds available. That is why members of this party were against assigning a specific amount of money to the board, as was done last session in amendments introduced by the then secretary of state.
Turning to my own area, I should like to refer shortly to a self help organization which has been set up there, known as the Pictou county research and development commission. This organization has now been incorporated under an act of the Nova Scotia legislature. It involves people in all walks of life, including businessmen, clergy and labour representatives, and it has been established in order to help solve the pressing problem of unemployment in the area. A pocket of unemployment has persisted there for some time.
My own intention now is to refer to measures which might assist the recovery of this area. In the course of the last budget debate the Minister of Finance stated that if the tax incentives which he had introduced did not help solve this problem, he did not know what would. That seemed to be finality as far as he was concerned. Perhaps I might be allowed to refer shortly to a speech made by Premier Stanfield of Nova Scotia in the Nova Scotia legislature on February 10 of this year. Before I do so I might mention that last year, I believe, I asked the then minister of transport, as the minister in charge of the Atlantic development board, what the respective roles of the development board and the area development agency would be. He pointed out, I believe, that the Atlantic development board would deal with the larger fields, such as transportation, power, and so on, whereas the area development agency would attempt to encourage the settlement of new industries. Mr. Stanfield, speaking in the Nova Scotia legislature, was reported as follows, and I am quoting from the Chronicle-Herald of February 11, 1964:
Premier Stanfield last night criticized the federal government for failing to provide sufficient tax incentives to bring industry to Nova Scotia.

Speaking in the throne speech debate in the legislature, the premier said his government understood the difficulty the federal government had in providing industrial incentives and added that it appreciated the location of a heavy water plant in Cape Breton.
He said federal tax incentives to industries locating in areas of heavy unemployment are not going to bring industry to Nova Scotia.
"Federal tax availability of such incentives in an area of heavy unemployment in central Canada may attract an industry we could otherwise have brought to some part of Nova Scotia," he said.
The premier went on to say:
We need more positive inducement, far less timidity and far more imagination from the federal government and its agencies.
I shall not quote any further on this occasion. No reference is made in that speech to any particular industry, but I know personally of an industry which would perhaps have gone into Pictou county had the tax incentives offered been sufficient. The tax holiday, and the other benefits, might well attract an industry to another part of Canada, as the premier indicated, rather than to a designated area of Nova Scotia.
Hon. members may ask, of course, what suggestions Premier Stanfield has to make. Well, those suggestions have been made, and they are in line with recommendations I myself put forward, or attempted to put forward, in the course of last session, as outlined in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald on February 12 in an editorial headed "New Policies". Part of this editorial states:
Notwithstanding the tone of finality with which Finance Minister Gordon introduced the tax incentives last June, should Ottawa be prevailed upon to grant additional tax favours on the basis of economic or political regions rather than by the sole yardstick of the present-district unemployment levels throughout Canada?
The article goes on:
Be that as it may, there may be a more practicable possibility: why not pool some of the uncommitted millions belonging to the Atlantic development board with those of such provincial development agencies as Industrial Estates Limited so that the latter can extend even more generous start-up assistance to industry?
That is one suggestion. Another question which has been asked is, of course, how flexible are the terms of reference governing the Department of Industry? Can this department, in co-operation with Industrial Estates, intercede with Ottawa for assistance in specific cases. The department has not been in existence for very long. Its directors are being paid good salaries as is necessary, I admit, if we are to have the services of good men. I hope they will not sit on their fannies here in Ottawa, but that they will get out into areas such as mine and work together with agencies such as Industrial Estates and the Pictou county research and development commission, so as to find some solution to

the unemployment problem which faces us. This is a labour surplus area and it is one that should be tackled first. I have made some inquiries since coming to Ottawa for this session and I am advised it is possible that the area development agency will have district offices, perhaps provincial and perhaps maritimewise; I do not know which. I hope the government will make this clear, and I hope the new Department of Industry will get to work on this question and will not just be another department sitting here in Ottawa. I put a question to the right hon. Prime Minister the other day and asked him to direct the attention of the area development agency to my own area, and I hope this will be done.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I could refer for just a moment to the question of railway cars which are manufactured by Eastern Car Company in my constituency, which is the largest employer in that area. The orders have not been sufficient in the last decade, as was pointed out the other day, to keep this plant and its labour force going sufficiently to provide full employment. Suggestions have been made through the years since I have been here, and before that undoubtedly, that orders from the C.N.R. particularly, being a crown corporation, and the C.P.R. should be placed at a time which will provide sufficient winter employment rather than summer employment. In that way it would provide work at a time when it is most urgently needed.
I know there are problems in this connection. I know, for instance, that the two chief railways of Canada are now carrying out research into new types of cars. Only a year or two ago they brought out a new type of insulated car. I have reference to Track magazine, published by Canadian National Railways for their employees, wherein is an article regarding two new types of cars with which they are now experimenting. One is the "Prairie Schooner" and the other is the "Hy-Beam". The Schooners are essentially canvas covered gondola cars used to carry such products as stainless steel and other high quality metal products. The Hy-Beam car will be used to ship packaged lumber and will have other advantages also. I realize that in order to compete with other forms of transportation our two chief railways have to carry out research as to the type of car that is needed by different manufacturers, and so on. However, I hope some system can be worked out to provide for this work being done at the right time.
While I was at home between sessions objections were made to the use of a large number of United States cars, especially to carry P.E.I. potatoes to domestic markets. At that time the C.N.R. said the United States
The Address-Mr. MacEwan cars were all right, but the ratio of their use is 20 to 1 for every Canadian car. My recommendation to the government, through the Minister of Transport, is that they should look into this matter to see if these cars are of a suitable type, and also whether more Canadian cars could be used, thereby helping out the manufacturers in Canada, not only the car companies but those who manufacture the components, whose plants are situated all over the country.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I hope the government will continue giving longer term credit in regard to our exports, and perhaps they will even look into the possibility of providing railway cars, as has been suggested, to some of the underdeveloped countries in the world today.
Finally, Mr. Speaker-I believe I have almost run out of time-may I refer briefly to the amendment which has been moved by this party on the matter of the extension of family allowances to age 18. I recall asking the right hon. Prime Minister during the last session whether an extension to age 18 would be brought in during that session. At that time my question caused a little flurry because everyone was a little upset and tempers were short. The right hon. Prime Minister said that if we got on with the business they would be able to bring forward things like that. We are now through with that session and into a new one, and it still has not been done. I believe that in many areas of Canada, those in the lower income category, this matter is very important. Such an extension would provide money for older children to age 18 who are remaining in school. Education is important, and I think all members of this house should certainly back the amendment of this party on the vote this evening.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I refer to the matter of votes. I heard a certain correspondent on the C.B.C. the other morning saying that the Conservative party were of course trying to put the government out of power, and this was not right because the people of Canada did not want another election, and so on. Of course there were others who spoke before, who said there were not sufficient members on this side of the house to give the government a run for their money -and we are still wrong. My suggestion is that on the question of voting-I am referring to the matter of the sales tax and the amendment that is now before the house-this party has a perfect right to bring these things forward. We are a responsible opposition, and will continue to bring these things forward in spite of what some people say.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not going to take any notice of the chit chat from over there. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am sure hon. members opposite will want me to retire before I have finished this afternoon, as I am not going to sit silent in this house when I consider that Canada is being sold down the river because of the terms of this treaty, particularly when we sell our power for 30 years and our water forever.
On January 30, 1964 a petition was started by the mayor of Nelson, a fine young chap full of ambition who was recently elected, and the Nelson chamber of commerce which read as follows:
Petition of urgency. We, the undersigned citizens of the East and West Kootenay, province of British Columbia, hereby petition your government to place before the house as the first order of business the immediate ratification of the treaty on the Columbia river development signed by yourself and the President of the United States in Washington, D.C., on January 22, 1964, which has our wholehearted support. This petition is sponsored by Kootenay chambers of commerce.
It did not mention how many chambers. This petition, Mr. Speaker, was launched with front page fanfare on February 1 in the Nelson Daily News, which proclaimed that the objective was 10,000 signatures from the East and West Kootenays. I am glad to see the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) in the house.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am pleased to hear that, but the hon. gentleman is just using this tactic to divert the attention of the house from the painful position he is in. This activity was carried on for a few days with press announcements claiming great success,

and saying many communities in the East and West Kootenays were signing the petition. Some 1,500 to 2,000 copies of this petition were distributed in Kootenay West and Kootenay East to every businessman and other persons who would accept them. Officials of the Social Credit party in some communities campaigned from door to door for three weeks. Then the press announcements turned to editorial complaints that people were not signing the petition, and the public was openly criticized for not rallying to the cause. Finally, on the day the petition was sent to Ottawa one had to turn to the inside pages of the Nelson Daily News to discover, under a small column heading, that only 3,542 signatures were actually obtained.
The petition was wired to the Prime Minister on the opening day of parliament over the Western Union telegraph lines. I was always under the impression that you could get in touch with Ottawa by wire from Nelson through the C.P.R. telegram service, but apparently they were so ashamed of the result that they sent the wire over Western Union telegraph lines, with a grand total of 3,542 signatures to the petition.
What I want to bring to the attention of the house is this; that there are over 57,000 persons in Kootenay East and Kootenay West over 18 years of age, and also that many of 18 years of age signed this petition, including some people from the coast and other points. I am informed that at the time the petition was sent, Kimberley and Invermere were not included; but I understand that this small number of additional signatures would not have made any material difference. I hope the hon. member for Kootenay East will tell us the figures for Kimberley when they come in; I have already heard the magnificent total. Anyway, the petition was a flop.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have been asked by some members of the New Democratic party and some Liberals and Conservatives in my constituency to seize every opportunity to bring to the attention of the people of Canada how they have been misled by official statements on the Columbia treaty by the government. The basic issue with the Columbia treaty is whether the current agreement represents proper use of a great Canadian resource. There is growing evidence that control of and benefits from this national asset have been turned over to a foreign power. Almost as disturbing is evidence that government mismanagement of this resource is being concealed from Canadians by the governments of Canada and British Columbia. A number of official government statements on the Columbia are now known to be completely untrue. The magnitude of these deceits and
The Address-Mr. Herridge false promises and claims, and the fact that some of them have officially emanated from no less a source than the office of the Prime Minister, indicate development of a political deceit of prime importance.
Now I am going to give some specific examples of misrepresentation, broken promises and deceit. They are so awful, Mr. Speaker, that they stick in my throat and I must take a drink of water.
Before they came to power the Liberals often stated that this treaty was defective and must be renegotiated. Yes, we all listened to the hon. member for Kootenay East denounce the treaty. The record is replete with the criticism of hon. members opposite. The Prime Minister himself said that a Liberal government would develop a treaty which General McNaughton could support.
Second, during the election the Prime Minister promised in writing that no action would be taken by a Liberal government before consultations with the people concerned. I should like to quote from a letter he wrote to Mr. Donald C. Waterfield, chairman of the water resources committee, Nakusp chamber of commerce, Nakusp, B.C.: Dear Mr. Waterfield:
Your letter of April 12th has just arrived and I would like to assure you that I agree with you that it is imperative to renegotiate the Columbia river treaty.
May I also assure you that all B.C. interests particularly those of the water resources committee of Nakusp chamber of commerce, will be consulted by a new Liberal government before a final decision is reached.
Were they consulted? They never heard anything more from the Prime Minister; and when the Secretary of State for External Affairs flew over the Arrow lakes he made certain that the plane flew at a good elevation above that community. He did not want to see those people. Anyway, not a word was heard. The Prime Minister of Canada broke his written promise to those people and to many others in my constituency.
Third, because of their belief that the government would support General McNaugh-ton's plan the Liberal association of Kootenay West offered General McNaughton the nomination, I am told under the spurring of the hon. member for Kootenay East, or shall I say at the suggestion of the hon. member for Kootenay East. I was informed of this by West Kootenay Liberals. However, General McNaughton would not consider running; he did not want to enter into the political field at his age.
Fourth, Liberal candidates strongly criticized the treaty and the construction of the high Arrow dam. I was at five all-party meetings with the Liberal candidate in my riding in which he condemned the high

The Address-Mr. Herridge Arrow dam, as a result of which the Liberal party got the highest number of votes it has had in Kootenay West for 25 years, and this as the result of deceiving the people. That is a fact.
The attacks on the ability of General McNaughton by Mr. Williston and Dr. Keenleyside have included false statements and disparaging remarks about General McNaughton's professional judgment. I am hurrying along, Mr. Speaker, because they have committed so many crimes in connection with this treaty that it is hard to tell them all in 30 minutes. Mr. Williston stated in the British Columbia legislature that General McNaughton had had no practical experience in hydro development, and hence was not qualified to speak on the Columbia. He was given an honorary membership in the Alberta engineering institute, and in his certificate it refers to "this eminent engineer, researcher", and so on and so forth. This is a strange opinion about one of the principal architects of the St. Lawrence developments and of all other Canadian and United States water projects between 1950 and 1961, including the Columbia itself.
Now, what did Mr. Williston do? In his speech to the legislature of February 7 last year he said that a man like General McNaughton should be in substantial agreement. He said:
Both groups are attempting to squeeze every last ounce of political advantage out of a man who has made his mark, is now past his prime, never has been an acknowledged hydraulics engineer, and now stands alone abandoned to his own support of resources even against the expressed stand of those technical men who a short time ago reported to him in the course of their duties.
Then he went on to make other remarks about General McNaughton which are entirely inaccurate, and which will be put before the external affairs committee.
Now I come to Dr. Keenleyside. He has often said that no other expert in a position to understand the Columbia supports the general's views. This is a completely false statement. As evidence I mention a partial list of those who have said that the treaty is a poor deal for Canada: Mr. E. G. Cass-Beggs, Saskatchewan Power Corporation; Professor J. F. Muir, head of the civil engineering department at the University of British Columbia; Mr. R. Deane, who is senior electrical engineer of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company-I must be exact and say he is speaking for himself-Mr. L. Higgins of the Ontario hydro, who also is expressing his personal views; Mr. F. J. Bartholomew, consultant on the Columbia and the builder of a good many projects in and out of

Canada. I can think of at least a dozen others, but time will not permit me to mention them.
Sixth, the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources has sent to many individuals who have asked for information on the treaty a copy of a newspaper article dated January 24,	1963, from the Vancouver
Province, a paper which then supported Premier Bennett and the treaty. This article is full of half truths and out of context quotations, but northern affairs has stated that it represents a true expression of government views. This article was promoted by the present clerk of the privy council. In addition, a very nice letter from Gordon Robertson, who was at that time deputy minister, to Paddy Sherman assisted him to obtain a literary award. One might say this was obviously a mutual benefit society. Then there are letters from Mr. J. D. McLeod, chief engineer of the water resources branch, telling people that this article is objective and true and so on. Others were written by Mr. G. M. MacNabb, who said in one letter dated February 15, 1963:
It is brief but accurate in all important aspects.
Did you ever hear of a government department, Mr. Speaker, using a newspaper article to sell a bill of goods?
Seventh, comparative prices of power from the Peace and Columbia have been flagrantly manipulated by the British Columbia government according to its immediate objective. To justify starting the Peace it issued an engineering report showing that Peace power would be cheaper than Columbia power, by the simple device of ignoring flood control on the Columbia. Now, to justify the Columbia Mr. Williston has reversed his position and is saying that Columbia power is 25 per cent cheaper. If this is true, Premier Bennett is exporting the bulk of this cheap power to the United States while imposing expensive Peace power on British Columbia. I am told by competent engineers that over the next 30 years this one mill difference will cost the people of British Columbia $393 million in extra and higher hydro charges.
I get these figures from the report on the Columbia and Peace power projects published by the British Columbia energy board. I am very pleased, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) is here this afternoon. He has been absent for some time today, but I am glad I have attracted his attention in discussing this matter in the house.
Eighth, the government has stated that downstream benefits are split 50-50. In fact Canada gets only about 40 per cent under this deal, but I am not going to deal with

the technical aspects. We will leave that to the men who come before the committee.
Ninth, the government claims that Canada gets $501 million under the treaty. This is not true. The sale price for downstream benefits is $274 million. If this were invested instead of spent on construction it would be worth $501 million in 10 years and a trillion dollars if the calculation were extended for several more decades. The $501 million statement is just as valid and just as meaningless as the statement that anyone who invested $1 at the time of our Lord would own the world today. Those are the mathematics of the people who have been boosting this treaty. No doubt if we invest the $274 million in 5 per cent bonds instead of building dams we will own the universe at the time of the millenium. This is what the Liberal party has been trying to do all along.
Tenth, the United States claims our downstream power is worth 3.75 mills. British Columbia claims that the figure is 5.3 mills. Both cannot be right, and the government calculations in the press release which purport to reconcile these figures cannot be substantiated from any documents.
Eleventh, the last clause of the protocol, which says that the treaty will not constitute a precedent, is dangerous nonsense. Any act is a precedent, regardless of whether or not it is called one, and the Columbia treaty is bound to have great influence on future water treaties. The frantic efforts of the government, particularly of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to convince the public that no precedent exists indicate that they regard it as a deal they would not wish to repeat. On the other hand, the United States is making equally strenuous efforts to establish the treaty as a change in the whole framework of Canada-United States water law. At the United States Senate Columbia hearings Richard Kearney of the United States state department had this to say, and I am about to quote from the hearings of the committee on foreign relations of the United States Senate:
-this treaty, for example, is going to be one of the major points of development for international law in this respect.
Then he went on to say:
However, I would say that the trend in international law is strongly toward the establishment of the principle that an upstream riparian state cannot deal with the waters within its borders which cross its boundary to a downstream riparian state in such a way as to seriously impair the rights or interests of the downstream riparian state.
Then he also said:
I think, senator, that this treaty will be considered as adding of that body of law.
The Address-Mr. Herridge
This is the attitude of these senators with respect to this matter. They consider that this establishes a precedent. Then we come to my twelfth point illustrating deceit and misleading information.
Twelfth, in its background to the protocol the government said:
Article XIII gives Canada the right to divert the Kootenay into the Columbia.
This is a completely false statement, and everybody knows it. The right has always been ours. They cannot give us any right. The treaty does not give us any such right but in fact takes away part of the unlimited right we have now and can legally and physically enforce if the control dams are situated in Canada.
Thirteenth, another illustration of misleading statements is the fact that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has repeatedly assured prairie leaders that Columbia waters can be diverted to the prairies when needed. This is a highly questionable statement. One clause does say we have the right, but other clauses make it legally and economically impossible ever to exercise it.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that when I reflect on the blunders of the government, and I listen to the speeches of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and read his letters to the people whom he has completely misled on this article of the treaty, it makes me think that the emblem of the Liberal party should be an eel rampant on a rhubarb leaf.

I want to deal with my fourteenth illustration of misleading statements. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano, widely accepted as the chairman of the power committee of the Liberal caucus, said in the house on December 12, 1962: 1, We must not agree to conditions which tie our hands with respect to the use of water in our territory; 2, the Libby project must be postponed if not eliminated; 3, projects involving flooding in Canada should be postponed. In his plan for action on the Columbia-I have a copy but I do not have time to read it- the hon. member for Coast-Capilano said that the treaty is unworkable and must be renegotiated. The public were clearly led to believe that this was the program of the Liberal party. There were articles in the Vancouver newspapers written by the member for Coast-Capilano which mentioned that the hon. gentleman was chairman of the B.C. power policy committee of the Liberal party.
There has been no such renegotiation. Far from any significant improvements, the protocol merely reinforces some of the clauses that were most destructive of Canada's interests. I have a copy here of a speech on the Columbia river made by the hon. gentleman on December 12. I have a copy of his plan of action for the Columbia which appeared in Ottawa on February 16, 1963, and which will bear out the fact that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano was one of the greatest criticis of the former government and the terms of the treaty as it was at that time.

The only improvement in this treaty from our point of view is that we have obtained a bit more cash for the power. One of the bad features of this treaty is that we have sold our cheap power from the Columbia to the United States on a firm basis for 30 years; that is one difference in this treaty.
I see that my time is going, and I overlooked mentioning the question of diversion. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has written to Premier Lloyd of Saskatchewan on this subject, and has sent telegrams. Here is a typical telegram from the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Read it, and then you will wonder what it means. Premier Lloyd replied on January 27, after reading the telegram from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, as follows:

X can only continue to conclude that the proposed treaty will in fact deny any possibility of the use of the water so far as the people of the prairie provinces are concerned.

speechtext: What is the date of that telegram?

January 27 of this year. I want to be fair in this connection, but I say without any equivocation that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has tried to mislead the people of Canada in respect of the right of diversion of the Columbia water for use on the prairies. Certainly, the treaty questions the right to divert for consumptive purposes, but the terms of a later clause prevent that. Let us be honest and frank about this and tell the people the truth.
I do not mind differing with people, but I do dislike this sleight of hand politics, and that is what we have been experiencing so far as this treaty is concerned.
I should like to give my fifteenth illustration with regard to the deception that has been practised by this government. These illustrations clearly indicate that a great deal of deception on the part of this government was deliberate, not caused by mere ignorance. Any doubt of this was finally removed on February 5, 1964 when a letter from the Prime Minister's office gave the following astonishing description of government tactics. I have a photostatic copy of a letter written by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister. I want hon. members to listen to this. He is writing to a prominent engineer in British Columbia who had written the hon. member criticizing certain features of the treaty. I quote:
You mentioned a cost estimate of $175 million for the high Arrow project. This is a new figure so far as I am concerned.

What does that mean? This means that from the Prime Minister's office there is an admission that the people and the press of' Canada have been given false information. There is no question about it.

speechtext:
I should like to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply at this time. I should like to make a few comments on the social security measures referred to in the speech from the throne, the ones that will be carried out in the near future, and to make a few recommendations for future social progress in connection with these measures.
In the last session of parliament we saw the old age pensions increased to $75 a month. A short while later, and in conjunction with the provinces, the blind, disabled and old age assistance pensions were increased a similar amount. In this session of parliament surely one of the first pieces of legislation to be considered must be the Canada pension plan. There is a great public interest in it, and I know hon. members have received many cards urging them to support the plan. We must implement it as soon as possible, and stop all further efforts to block or delay it. I am sure that in the very near future it will be referred to a special committee of the house.
My personal feeling is that this committee should sit every morning if necessary, to hear the many witnesses who will appear before it, so that the legislation can be returned to parliament for full consideration before the summer recess.
Another measure mentioned in the throne speech is the arrangements whereby university students who require financial assistance will be able to secure loans without payment of interest during their years of study. This is to be done in conjunction with the provinces, but I would like to point out that such aid is not new. Federal assistance has previously been given to university students. This was done after world war II when thousands of ex-servicemen and women went back to school to complete their education, under the auspices of the Department of Veterans Affairs.
With this federal assistance thousands of these people became skilled and highly-trained, and used their new education and abilities for the benefit of all Canadians. Surely the assistance that the federal government gave after the war can be provided in peacetime, so that education will depend on the ability and ambition to learn, and not on the ability to pay for it.

The Address-Mr. Harley
This loan program is the first step by which the government can help students. The next step will be the provision of scholarships, and we hope this will be introduced in the very near future. The Liberal party has advocated a scholarship plan, and the government is committed to it within the life time of a normal parliament.
In my opinion the third priority should be given to the extension of family allowances to the age 18, provided that the children remain at school. The amount of money involved per child does not seem large, yet I know it can mean the difference in many families as to whether schooling will be continued. Scholarships and bursaries at the university level are of little use if students do not finish their high school education, and this is one step the government can take to discourage high school drop-outs and encourage further education.
This brings me to a very brief statement I would like to make in connection with the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard). So that there will be no misunderstanding I want to put on the record a quotation from the policy of the Liberal party announced during the general election of 1963. Under the heading, "Opportunities for Youth," it states:
Extend lamily allowances from the age of 16 for boys and girls who remain students. This will help families to provide the best possible education for young Canadians and reduce the member of teenagers seeking unskilled jobs.
The only difference we have with the hon. member's amendment is one of timing.
This morning the hon. member for Me-gantic (Mr. Langlois) talked about government responsibility. Surely it is government responsibility to decide what the balance should be between what the needs of the Canadian people are and when the government can afford to meet them.
The next priority should be a medicare program. I am sure most people are aware that the royal commission on health services has not yet reported. I understand it will not do so before the spring, nor, indeed perhaps before summer, but, having commissioned this exhaustive and expensive study, it would be ridiculous to proceed with a medicare plan without awaiting the report and making a full study of its findings. With this basic information the government can then plan a suitable medicare plan for Canada, again in association with the provinces, to serve the needs of the Canadian people.
When he spoke the other day the hon. member for Hamilton South (Mr. Howe) mentioned a complete medicare program. I should like to point out very roughly what such a program would cost for one year. In

1960, the cost of medical care in Canada was approximately $400 million. In the same year the cost of drugs was almost as high, amounting to approximately $350 million. During the same period of time the cost of dental care was $90 million, and if the cost of other things were included, such as glasses, physiotherapy and medical appliances, the total would approach $1 billion for a complete medicare program for one year.
In this connection I would like to remind hon. members of what the Prime Minister said during the election campaign. He said that we were committed to a medical care program and that we would bring it forward when we could afford it, when the economy of the country was again satisfactory, probably in the third or fourth session of parliament. We in the Liberal party are still committed to that.
The medicare program which the Liberal party had in its platform reflected the commonly held view that certain groups and classes of people have more need of medicare assistance than other groups. With this thought in mind, the Liberal party program was that all school children be given free medicare, and also adults over age 65, and that all other adults would pay the first $25 per year of their own medical expenses and the government would pay the remainder. The next priority in that program was to be given to drugs and dental care, particularly for children.
I should like to go on record, along with one of the hon. members from Winnipeg, in saying that mental illness and tuberculosis should be included under the terms of the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. In the last ten years new treatments have been developed for these illnesses, but they are not included under the hospital act. We hear a great deal of talk that people should accept mental illness in the same way as they accept any other illness. Surely, if we expect the general public to treat mental illness and tuberculosis like any other illness, then the government should be prepared to do that first. Great progress has been made in the care of mental illness and of the mentally retarded, and I congratulate the government for holding a conference on mental retardation in Ottawa early this fall.
To summarize briefly what I have said, I hope the government will give consideration to social legislation in the following priority: first, a Canada pension plan; second, a loan plan for university students; third, the extension of family allowances to the age of 18 years and, fourth, a medicare program to serve the medical needs of the people of Canada.
