speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish at the outset to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, not so much for what they have said, but for the manner in which they performed their task. I extend to them my sincere congratulations.
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I should like to dwell on the awakening of Quebec. I know that expressions such as rebirth, evolution, awareness and even quiet revolution are now being used. But those are but a few terms to describe what is going on in Quebec, what has roused and stirred its people. Things are on the move in Quebec, in the economic as well as in the social field, in the field of education as well as in that of national aspirations.
Since the war the face of Quebec has undergone a drastic change. The shift of population to urban centres, started during the last conflict, has been maintained and even increased throughout the years. That shift has had deep repercussions on the population generally. A whole people found itself being thrown into the technological complex of this modern world and, as a result, the needs and requirements of education have become imperative.
The youth of French Canada is throwing itself headlong into the fields of science, business, finance and industry. Our universities, our schools of engineering, of science and technology are overflowing with students. Enrolments have doubled, tripled, quadrupled. On the other hand, our high schools are being rapidly brought up to date and new ones are springing up every day.
French Canadians have an obvious and legitimate desire to contribute to the economic development of their province and of the whole country. They want the French fact to get as full a recognition as possible in the other provinces and they want such recognition to be truly and generally acknowledged within all federal agencies.
Many of our politicians claim credit for that evolution and for that awakening. As far as I am concerned, I feel that this is a normal process on the part of a people which has kept its national identity even though it had to go through the worst vicissitudes on the North American continent. As a member from Quebec, I rejoice at that evolution and as a member of the parliament of Canada I feel that is the way things must work out within confederation.
Undoubtedly such an evolution could not take place without tremendous difficulties.
The Address-Mr. Balcer Let us take for instance the field of education. The budget which was brought down recently in the Quebec legislature provides for an expenditure of $415 million for education only, that is $2 or $3 million more than in Ontario. Our people are ready to make such sacrifices, but the thirst for knowledge on the part of our youth deserves to be encouraged.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be a prophet of doom and gloom. Yet, I must say that this fine upsurge is going through a rough time in Quebec because the federal government has failed to grasp its meaning.
All that renewal can of course be accomplished within confederation. To a large extent, the central government will be what we want it to be. If we French Canadians break away, if we must look on it as an enemy, if it polarizes all our frustrations, well, we can expect nothing from it. On the other hand, if we join with it, if we feel we are called upon to play our full part in that government, while standing firm on principles and accommodating on procedures, we can derive from it all the advantages which normally should come to us.
Confederation is not unchangeable. It is evident that after a century of life, alterations and adjustments must be made. What must be safeguarded is the spirit which prevailed when it was worked out. Confederation which has rendered such great service was conceived in a spirit of conciliation by the two great races of this country. Of course, that document needs streamlining. There surely must be a way to do it through good will on both sides.
It would be a tragedy to leave the initiative to extremists, and I think that this federal government, because of its irresolution and lack of energy and vision in that field, runs the risk of giving them more importance.
The future of our ethnic group can certainly not be left in the hands of extremists like the Liberal member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Cho-quette) who never fails to insult English speaking Canadians in what is dearest to them. It cannot be left in the hands of the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), who would refuse the French language the right to exist outside Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, never have federal-provincial relations been so bad and never has there been a Quebec provincial government less understood by the Ottawa government. Yet, how we have heard that old refrain: Grits in Quebec, Grits in Ottawa. It is even the theme of all the discussions of the Quebec Liberal federation. It is even the theme of a great debate between the partisans of the Hon. Rene Levesque and those of our friends opposite.

The Address-Mr. Balcer What can come out of that discussion? It can simply cause in federal provincial relations an uneasiness which must be cleared away at any price.
The lack of understanding of the present Liberal government when confronted with the claims of the French Canadians is reflected by the measure to provide assistance to municipalities and the one relating to the pension fund. The Liberal government in Ottawa tried to impose those two anticonstitutional measures by disregarding the acknowledged priority right of the provinces in that field. But in both cases, it had to yield to the protests of public opinion in Quebec after hastily convening federal-provincial conferences, during which it had to admit the inconsistency of its centralizing trend. In spite of the high-sounding name of co-operative federalism used by the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) to term those strategic retreats, he will not succeed, in my opinion, in fooling anybody.	.
In support of this allegation, allow me to quote from an article by Messrs. Richard Daigneault and Dominique Clift published in La Presse the day before yesterday and which reads as follows:
The federal project of scholarships for university students has just shown the worthlessness of the concept of co-operative federalism to Quebec officials who firmly believed in it.
Following federal-provincial conferences held in the capital in 1963, Ottawa had given to understand that in future, the federal government would no longer introduce measures coming under provincial jurisdiction without previous consultation with the provinces.
The promise was made that there would be no more walking into the neighbour's house without knocking.
Co-operative federalism was, so to speak, to introduce a certain etiquette, a certain courtesy, in the relationship between Ottawa and the provinces.
And Messrs. Daigneault and Clift concluded as follows:
In Toronto, the surprise is similar; Ottawa announces that it will immediately proceed with the Canada pension plan and that the new plan will be implemented this year.
Premier John Robarts feels that, once again, Ottawa is acting high handedly with him.
In other words, co-operative federalism seems to be a rather mysterious reality. At the moment, it has very few supporters, either in Quebec city or in Toronto.
In addition, Mr. Vincent Prince, in La Presse of Wednesday, February 28, 1964, under the title "Infringement by consent?"- such is the definition given by Mr. Prince to the highsounding formula of the Secretary of State-wrote this:
Could it be that, under the guise of co-operative federalism, Ottawa is trying to thrust on us "infringement by consent"?
This question is not as idle as it may seem at first sight. At least, when considering the action of the federal government of late.

One has only to recall last year's legislation allowing Ottawa to grant loans to municipalities. Or, better still, the federal measure now under discussion regarding financial assistance to students.
In our humble opinion, this is not federalist co-operation, but an infringement of federalism itself.
And further Mr. Prince goes on to say:
And the provinces, labouring under an unfair distribution of fiscal revenue, are agreeing to that. They have no alternative.
True, Quebec enjoys some consideration. But, by the same token our province is considered as a special case, becomes an object of suspicion. This is irritating, and odious in the long run.
Mr. Speaker, the tax agreements entered into last November are another evidence of the inertia of the present government in connection with federal-provincial relations. These fiscal agreements are merely a rehash. No proposal other than a few timid amendments to formulas already existing, was made for a new plan aimed at tackling the root of the problem.
There will undoubtedly be a new conference in March but then again, the Liberal government will have nothing new to propose. It has not altered its philosophy and will only be trying to maintain its stand and impose to the province of Quebec the status quo which is undermining the very foundation of confederation.
The present federal government, following the centralizing and unconstitutional tactics of the late Mackenzie King and his bureaucrats, who are now ministers of the crown, continues to display a systematic contempt for the federative pact, for the basic rights and needs of the provinces. Moreover, there is nothing in the speech from the throne which acknowledges the fair requests of the province of Quebec and French Canada in the constitutional, fiscal, financial, economic, industrial and educational fields. On the contrary, the Liberal government advocates the granting of student loans without previous consultation, a measure which undermines the exclusive rights of the province in that field, which increases the disagreement between the two great races of Canada and which widens the gap which separates them.
Such an autocratic policy by the present government only adds fuel to the grievances raised by the province of Quebec and French Canada. Men like the Secretary of State speak on the one hand of saving the Canadian confederation and, on the other hand, the same men continuously take steps which destroy the spirit and the letter of the confederative pact. Those are, Mr. Speaker, the actual people who are responsible to a great extent for the national misunderstanding and the present restlessness in Quebec.

In view of the crucial problems which now require a direct, frank and definite dialogue between the two great founding races of our [DOT]country and the other Canadians, the time has come to answer two main questions: what is the complaint of Quebec and of the French *Canadians, and what do they want exactly?
Mr. Speaker, we, French Canadians, admit that the Canadian confederation to which we agreed in 1867, had happy results in a number of fields. It gave us a Canadian sovereignty, enabled us to build up a domestic and foreign trade, to co-ordinate administrative .services, to develop a well-known national defence policy, to ensure monetary and banking uniformity, and to gain international prestige.
But all that cannot make us forget that true federalism was not always practised, for the sharing of sovereignty between the central .government and the provincial governments was not respected. The fact that those various governments were to remain co-ordinated and not subordinated was overlooked. Provincial rights and needs were not sufficiently respected following wars and economic crises, and so the setting up of true federalism in Canada has not succeeded.
For true federalism, as distinct from a purely superficial federalism, requires that the lines of authority and the fields of taxation be clearly defined.
The French Canadian of 1964 is impatient and does not tolerate easily the status quo, and here is why: the standard of living today of the average Quebecker is found to be 10 per cent lower than that of the average Canadian, and 28 per cent lower than the average in Ontario. We manage hardly 5 per cent of the Canadian economic activity, while our ethnical group accounts for 29 per cent of the Canadian population.
In the province of Quebec itself, our group accounts for 82.6 per cent of the population but we manage only 10 per cent of the economic activity and hold only 20 per cent of the key positions. Our unemployed make up 40 per cent of all the unemployed in Canada.
Our 1963 average per capita income amounts to $1,700 whereas it is $2,000 in Ontario and $2,600 in the United States. Although France and Belgium suffered tremendous losses during the two world wars, their average per capita income amounts to $1,750 and $1,850.
Within the federal civil service, the part played by the French Canadians remains uncertain and unsatisfactory. The standards of eligibility reflect a concept that does not tally with our own school training, with the result that in the discharge of their duties, our
* The Address-Mr. Balcer compatriots often have to give up their mother tongue. Yet, in 1867, the idea was to build a bilingual, biethnical and bicultural Canada.
Among the federal civil servants earning $5,000 and more a year, French Canadians make up only 10 per cent of the total, according to a report published by the federal Department of Finance in 1960.
Moreover, my compatriots are kept out of the economic life by Ottawa, as there are practically none of them on or in the financial, industrial and commercial boards and departments of the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, I am voicing those complaints not to create misunderstanding, but rather to make the federal government realize what Quebec expects from it. It wants the federal government to assume its responsibilities.
Now, what do the French Canadians want? Well, Quebec and French Canada want more than subsidies and loans. They want the French fact and the English fact to be recognized once and for all in Canada as the two pillars on which the Canadian structure rests. We want to be full citizens in the rest of Canada as well as in Quebec.
In that respect I support the views expressed recently by Mr. Douglas How, editor in chief of the Canadian Reader's Digest. Here is part of what he said about the French Canadian nation when he spoke at the Queen Elizabeth hotel in the course of a visit to Montreal on October 16, 1963:
It is not surprising that such a people is awakening with a vengeance. The surprising fact is that it did not do so long ago. And the main thing, for the whole of Canada, is to find a solution, a way to channel this new energy and aggressivity in order to make such progress that would be fair to that people and advantageous for all.
Mr. Speaker, we want to play in Canada a dynamic role but understood and agreed on by all and to the advantage of all.
It is my firm belief that our problems will find a solution in the operation and implementation of true federalism, not a patched-up, hypocritical and deceptive federalism, such as the one devised by our hon. friends opposite. In spite of their shilly-shallying, singing the tune about a new federalism, a co-operative federalism, it is nothing else than camouflage and, in fact, accepted centralization. Those jugglers with the deficient Canadian policy, at the domestic level, invite the provinces to a meeting but insist on retaining nearly of the whole pile of money and offer only ridiculous bits under pressure and after concessions.
As long as such centralizers claim that Ottawa must assume the leadership of the whole Canadian economy and control the taxation of the various governments, the Canadian federation will be in danger.

The Address-Mr. Balcer
I should like to call the attention of the house to an editorial which appeared in the Montreal Gazette, on Wednesday, February 26, where we read:

What, then, is to happen if Quebec (like other provinces) finds itself facing these two hard facts: (a) there is no prospect that the rate of spending in the essential provincial fields of education, health and roads can be curtailed; on the contrary, the explosion will continue: (b) bigger and bigger deficits and bigger and bigger borrowing cannot continue indefinitely, as revenues repeatedly fall short of needs.
Is it not true that federal spending, in the years after the war (when revenues were buoyant and surpluses hard to hide) became quite excessive? Is this not the time for the emphasis to be switched in favour of provincial spending, and for the relative curtailment of federal? And should this curtailment not be exercised, in particular, in regard to any new large spending projects in the federal field?
Education, health and roads-are these not national, as well as the provincial responsibilities, in the sense that the need to make way for provincial spending in these imperative fields should become a national responsibility?

Mr. Speaker, the government should weigh its words carefully and realize that education must play a major role in the Canada of 1964. The federal government must not hesitate to extend the taxation powers of the provinces to enable them to meet their obligations in certain fields which will determine the future of our country.
Mr. Speaker, we are going through difficult times. It is important that the two great founding races of our country should soon come loyally closer and that the Canadian constitution be not only repatriated but also adapted to the evolution and to the problems that have to be faced in 1964.
Personally, I would suggest that the Canadian Senate be appointed as a special committee on the Canadian constitution. It is the proper body to study, within the framework of the federal parliament, our acute difficulties.
Indeed, prior to 1867, when the advisability of creating the upper chamber was discussed, it was decided that it should be entrusted with the task of representing every class of the Canadian society and protecting the rights of the provinces and of the minorities.
Consequently, I believe that the present government would be well advised to ask the Senate to establish a committee to study the means of bringing our constitution up to date, while respecting provincial rights and also to study the development opportunities for the provinces in their own fields, particularly the education field.
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago, the member for Kenogami-Jonquiere-

He disposed of the theory of the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), but he also put forward his own theory which in my opinion, embodies the present concept of the French speaking Canadians in Quebec on the problems now confronting them. I quote:
Canada is made up, as we can see, of two major cultural groups. Even though many other groups have enriched our national life for a century, each of those two initial groups retains, in 1964, in addition to its historical rights, a numerical strength and an institutional identity that entitle it to special recognition within the political framework of the country.
The partisans of this school of thought insist on certain concrete objectives which appear urgent to them. They request a broad autonomy for Quebec, the recognition of French in federal institutions and in the educational systems of all the provinces, and a greater participation by French Canadians in the management of the economic life.
But for the supporters of this school of thought, the objectives mentioned above may be reached within a flexible federation. Several persons within this group distrust, so to speak, political frameworks too rigidly based on so-called national realities. They prefer broader political frameworks which take into consideration not only race and culture, but also geography, not only past history which was simpler and more homogeneous, but also living history that resists every over-simplified effort to interpret it.
Mr. Speaker, I call the attention of the house to that editorial which, in my opinion, expresses the feelings of the public or at least of a great number of my fellow citizens from the province of Quebec.
I feel that by promoting unity and understanding between the two great races of our country, by helping each other and by respecting each others' rights, we will build a strong and united Canada, in other words a country where it is good to live.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like first of all to offer my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I think they did a very good job in carrying out the task assigned to them and they presented their positions well; it is not an opportunity

which is afforded to everyone. While we who sit on the opposition benches have very many opportunities which the backbenchers on the government side do not have, these are two which are offered to those who support the treasury benches.
I should like to take the opportunity to congratulate the new ministers and parliamentary secretaries on their appointments. I think they can look forward to at least a few months of very useful work and service to Canada.
Since I last spoke in this house, Mr. Speaker, there has come to my attention the passing of a great Canadian. This man, who was a senator from the Cariboo, Senator Tur-geon, was indeed in my view one of the great Canadians of his time. We were very sorry indeed to hear of his passing and we know that the efforts he put forward in his political and private life have left behind a real contribution to Canada and its people.
I should also like to take this opportunity to wish Mr. Walter Henderson, commonly known as Gus Henderson, a speedy recovery. I understand he has not been too well in the last few months. I am sure every member of the house who knew Mr. Henderson will want to join with me in expressing our best wishes to him for a speedy recovery.
The speech from the throne offers to the individual member an opportunity to brag a bit about his own constituency. In summation of the remarks I am about to make, may I say I have really got something to brag about. Cariboo constituency has the honour of being one of the most forward looking and progressive constituencies in Canada today. In fact, to a great extent the eyes of Canada are turned on it.
I should like now to refer to paragraph 11 in the speech from the throne, which is in these words:
At home there has been a heartening expansion of the economy. Employment has increased at an accelerated rate and the number of Canadians seeking work has fallen.
I should like to point out that the growth we are experiencing in Canada today is largely the result of the strong and aggressive provincial governments we have at this time. In the federal field we must see at all times that policies are adopted which will enhance their opportunities and make more readily available to the provinces opportunities for such expansion and acceleration. Strong, dynamic provincial leadership has led western Canada into a very important role in the economic life of the nation.
As a matter of fact, while I do not like quoting figures, it has been brought to my attention that British Columbia bought no less than $600 million worth of goods from
The Address-Mr. Leboe the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Last year this must be a very important development as far as Ontario and Quebec are concerned. In other words, we are interdependent as provinces but the important thing in our provincial set-up is that we should have the opportunity to meet the demands that are put upon us with the result that we will not have all our eggs in one basket.
We have 10 provinces and if the provincial governments are given the opportunity to expand and to put dynamic policies into operation this will bring about a situation where we will not have to worry so much about the economic problems facing us in Canada today. The fact that British Columbia is planning to make application for a part interest in a bank, probably to be known as the bank of British Columbia, indicates the forward thinking and forward steps being taken today in order to facilitate the expansion and growth of Canada.
The constituency of Cariboo is a highly diversified area. We have gold mines at Wells. We have great quantities of mercury at Pin-chy lake in the Fort St. James area. In the Quesnel area we have what are known as diatomaceous earth mines. Prince George is known as the white spruce capital of the world. It has been said that we ship enough lumber out of Prince George every year to build a city the size of Edmonton. A trainload of 120 to 140 cars of lumber, not the 35 or so cars of a few years ago, leaves Prince George 365 days a week-a year. That is a good long week. You would think I was from Texas.
So far as agriculture is concerned, we have the great agricultural area of the Peace river country which has had wheat kings on a number of occasions. There is also diversified mixed farming in the area around Prince George. In the southern part of the constituency we have the great fringes of the cattle industry. So far as the tourist industry is concerned, Cariboo constituency offers anything a person could wish in the way of tourist travel. There are good paved highways and more are to come. In this connection I would remind the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) to see that the road between the town of Jasper and the western boundary of the park will be ready when the highway is completed between Prince George and McBride and also between the Jasper boundary and Kamloops. The minister had better see that his engineers get to work because when Mr. Gaglardi starts calling his signals-in fact he already has- there will be some dirt flying along that highway.
We have some new industries in Cariboo constituency which I should like to mention.

The Address-Mr. Leboe We have a new molybdenum mine in the Vanderhoof area. We have an 800 ton pulp and paper mill being constructed at Prince George by Canadian Forest Products, which will be the largest on the North American continent. Another pulp mill is also being promoted by B.C. Forest Products on the Parsnip river, some 100 miles from Prince George. At Fort Nelson we have a filtering plant being constructed which will head up a 30 inch gas line running some 200 miles to Chetwynd and connecting there with the pipe line running down to the southern part of the province and into the United States. I believe that the transporting of gas as far as California is now being contemplated.
Then there are other developments. The Pacific Great Eastern railway is being extended in the Summit lake region a distance of approximately 100 miles to Fort St. James. This will open up a lot of new country. This area is just being tapped and the people of the area are looking forward to a great expansion.
We also have the Peace river development project, one of the largest earth filled dams in the world. It rises some 600 feet above the bed of the river and will be about 1J miles long when completed. It has been said that there will be enough earth in the dam to build a wall from Halifax to Vancouver nine feet wide and 12 feet high. It is a large project. This is only a part of the hydro development in the province of British Columbia. We heard a discourse this afternoon on the Columbia river by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge). The hon. member regrets very much the proposals that are made to improve the Columbia river development, but the days of screaming without effective reasoning are gone. I am sure that when the chips are down we will not have any problem in getting ratification of the treaty in this House of Commons.
There was a cry about the diversion of the Columbia river. This matter is taken care of in the treaty. If the people of the prairies need a little extra water, and if we can get it over the mountains from British Columbia, we can send it along to them.
When I was in Saskatchewan I made a review of the Saskatchewan river dam. I should like to pay tribute to Mr. Tim Cooper who was very kind and considerate during that trip, and invited me to have a look at this particular development in Saskatchewan. I was interested in noting that while this was supposed to be an irrigation dam, hardly anyone said a word about irrigation. They were talking about the power that would result from this development, and I think they are right. I feel that irrigation is a

wonderful thing but I do believe that the power resulting from dam development is a very important part of the reasoning behind its construction.
I am not going to bother the house by outlining a lot of the problems I have in the Cariboo constituency. I can deal with them with the various ministers. However, there are a few things I should like to mention that are urgent. While I believe we are making progress, I should like to take advantage of this opportunity by drawing to the attention of the house one or two things that could be done. First of all, we are looking forward to the construction of new airport terminals, particularly at Quesnel. The last time I was passing through Quesnel, when I got off the plane they trotted out the baggage buggy. A man was making out tickets using the baggage buggy as a desk. There are no facilities there and they are badly needed.
A few minutes ago I referred to the Jasper park road. I should like to see the government give consideration to the right of way through these national parks. I am told by trucking firms that it is more difficult to go through a national park with a truckload of goods than it is to go into the United States and come back. This situation should not exist. This is all Canada. We have a park straddling the only road that passes through the mountains in the vicinity of Jasper or Banff, and we expect the truckers to act as though they were entering into a new country when they enter these national parks. This is foolishness. I should like to see the government take steps to make arrangements with the provinces to have a right of way established through these parks so we can travel from point A to point B without being disturbed.
There is another thing I should like to mention which affects the whole of Canada but I shall refer to the Cariboo constituency in my remarks. I am thinking of private and municipal airports. In the Cariboo constituency we have some 40 private and municipal airports. These things grow like Topsy. A man will decide he wants a little plane, so he carves out an airstrip some 2,500 feet long. After he has it in good working condition, he finds that there are other people coming in and out of there almost every week. He puts gasoline there for himself. Sometimes he finds a note on the barrel saying, I am sorry; here is my name and address, but I had to borrow some of your gasoline. He has a plane, but he has no gasoline. These things happen.
What we need is a clear, forward looking policy in connection with municipal and private airports throughout Canada. When I am

speaking of airports I am including those float plane bases to which small aircraft can come on floats.
I am going to turn for a moment to the question of redistribution as it affects the Cariboo constituency. I believe most hon. members understand that an electoral district the size of Cariboo is too large for one man to service adequately. The Cariboo constituency has an area of about 121,000 square miles. It is over one third of the area of British Columbia and it is over one third of the area of the province of Ontario. In 1961 there were 20 constituencies in the province of Ontario with populations under 50,000. In 1961 there were about 20 constituencies in the province of Quebec under 50,000 population. In 1961 the Cariboo constituency had a population of about 84,000. Constituencies in British Columbia are generally larger in population than any group of constituencies in the whole of the Dominion of Canada. I should like to emphasize that we need redistribution based on three factors which are important: population, geography and topography.
It has been said that urban constituencies should get a large representation under special arrangement. I want to say that urban ridings do not have one tenth the problems of rural ridings so far as a member is concerned. You cannot find me an urban constituency which has a problem in connection with cleaning out rivers for fish or a post office because post offices have been established there for some time. There are no problems in connection with water diversion or highways because highways are municipal affairs so far as the urban member is concerned. I hope that when we consider the matter I will be on the committee on privileges and elections to do battle for the rural constituencies, to see that they get "a fair shake", if I may use that term.
Now, I cannot conclude my remarks without mentioning sugar. I have received a good many letters in respect of this matter of sugar prices. I am only going to take the time at this moment to mention the fact that the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) dealt with this for our group on Monday night. I think he did a very good job indeed of putting forth the position of our group in connection with this sugar problem. I believe that the price rise we had-I am not talking about the highest price-has been helpful to the Canadian sugar industry. There is no doubt of it. However, there is need for an over-all federal policy so far as sugar is concerned.
I should like to make a few remarks about this business of a national flag. We really get into deep water when we start talking about a national flag, I realize that. I think the solution lies in having a committee set
The Address-Mr. Leboe up that will choose perhaps four or five designs out of the some 2,500 or 2,900 designs that have been submitted, and put these on a ballot. They should include the red ensign, and should be put to a referendum of the people, with a transferable vote, so that each individual would choose the first, second, third, fourth and fifth in the order he preferred and, by the process of elimination, we will then have over 50 per cent of the people voting in favour of a particular flag. That will take all of us off the hook and put the responsibility where it belongs, on the shoulders of the people.
If it has been important enough to have waited 100 years to have the flag question settled, then let us take a little time to hold a plebiscite, and allow the people of Canada to settle it.
With regard to the workings of parliament itself, I believe that the question period is the most abused time in the house. There will have to be some self-discipline by the house, with a clearcut understanding of what questions should be. This would give the Speaker something to work with and cut down on a lot of the repetitious questions and the prodding which follows and has no real purpose. I think we had a serious situation in the matter of the stealing of armaments but in the last few days has this not been carried far beyond the realm of reason in the taking up of the time of the house? I would like to see a certain period of time set aside for questions. If we assemble at 2.30 o'clock, there should be a specific time at which the question period is cut off. At present we have got completely away from the intention of the question period.
I would also like to see some limitation of debate set out in the rules of the House of Commons, so that a debate can be ended by the Speaker by virtue of that rule. Further, I do not think we should have these resolutions, that precede money bills. They are a waste of time. Certainly they give us a little broader scope, but we do not need that because the second reading stage gives us all the latitude we need to deal with the matters in question.
I would also like to see the committees of the house set up for the lifetime of a parliament, without having to be reconstituted every session. Already we have the procedure whereby a motion can be made in the house removing an hon. member or an hon. lady from a committee and substituting the name of someone else. This is done all the time, and I cannot see any sense in the present method of appointing committees on a sessional basis.
Another matter which concerns me very much is the want of confidence motions. The

The Address-Mr. Tremblay manner in which they are handled at present is pretty unsatisfactory, and the people of the country are going to get so fed up that they will demand a set election date, a set time for the calling of an election. They will not stand for this sort of nonsense forever.
At present we have supporters of phony want of confidence motions saying, for example, that if you vote against a motion on family allowances, then you are voting against family allowances. What could be further from the truth? It is a want of confidence in the government, and that is all. If we have one want of confidence motion in the course of the debate on the speech from the throne it is enough. So far as I am concerned this is purely nonsense, and I would like to see all confidence motions confined to the debate on the throne speech, the budget, and one supply motion. As I say, if we do not do something about this the people will demand that we set a specified election date.

I notice my time is just about up, so I will close my remarks by asking that the government give consideration to the points I have mentioned. I think they are reasonable and I believe they are points with which the people of Canada will agree. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, if we were to take a cross section vote of the people I think they would say we are not accomplishing the things they feel we ought to accomplish.

speakeroldname: Hon. Rene Tremblay (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like those who preceded me, I would like to follow tradition by tendering my most sincere congratulations to the mover (Mr. Cote, Lon-gueuil) and seconder (Mr. Basford) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. That tradition, which I respect, as do all my fellow members, enables me to mention that one of them was French speaking and the other English speaking.
There is a tradition of long standing in this parliament, that the Speaker's function in the House of Commons and in the other place

is entrusted in turn to representatives of the two most important ethnic groups in this country.
According to another tradition, the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne are chosen among the representatives of the two most important racial groups in Canada.
We see, therefore, the Liberal party, which has been for a long time entrusted with the administration of this country, did always in its basic policy, wish to respect the fundamental rights of both the groups which founded this country.
The mover and seconder of the address have carried out their task most brilliantly, and I would like to commend them for it, following the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
Mr. Speaker, the tradition I just mentioned, which was even observed by the Conservatives, when they formed the government, is so fundamentally ingrained in this country that I was very much surprised to hear the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) state that it was something new on the part of the Liberal party to want to continue something already achieved and now called by the new name of co-operative federalism.
Mr. Speaker, that co-operative federalism is nothing new to the Liberal mind. It simply takes on a new shape in keeping with the problems now prevailing in this country.
I was also surprised to hear the hon. member for Three Rivers state that the Liberal government is a centralizing government, which is not in the least interested in provincial prerogatives. Yet, the as yet very brief history of this government, has been a constant co-operation with the provinces, in order to facilitate discussion not only of common issues but also of the problems which it very legitimately considered to exist with regard to the prerogatives and rights of the central government.
Conferences and meetings have taken place on taxation, and others will follow.
Almost every department had a conference, or will have one soon, with the provinces to discuss common problems. This is an indication of a firm will, on the part of this government, to associate the provinces and the municipalities in the gigantic task which confronts the governments, at all levels, as they try to bring back prosperity to our country.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that the hon. member for Three Rivers, as a former member of the Conservative government, had to draw a picture, a balance sheet of his party's administration. I realize that he had also to undertake to point out to us, Liberals, what

we should do to bring back to the country its unity and prosperity, which had been lost for too long.
In this house, I am the member for Mata-pedia-Matane, a constituency located in an area which, as everybody knows, has not been spoiled. It is a so-called "designated area", precisely because its numerous population until now was engaged mainly in farming and lumbering. Neither of these pursuits is actually very profitable, and there is a constant flow of emigration outside the area. The inhabitants of that constituency, as those of the whole Gaspe peninsula, wonder with anguish about their future.
Mr. Speaker, before the last election, I worked for the provincial administration. I decided to take an active part in politics and to come and give all possible assistance to the leader of the Liberal party, the present Prime Minister, and his colleagues.
I could have been a candidate in a Quebec City riding, where I live, but I preferred to go to an underdeveloped region in order to give new hope to the people and help them solve their problems.
What are those problems? They are similar to those in other underdeveloped sections of Canada. We have resources but they are untapped. Our people are hard working and courageous but there are not enough opportunities to earn a decent living. In short, we need special help from the federal or provincial government in order to give new impetus to our economy and to enable those people, who want to share the prosperity of the other sections of the country to improve their lot.
For my riding, as for the region as a whole, ARDA or rural development is the solution of the future.
I pay tribute to the Conservative ministers who, thanks to six years of work in the field of agriculture developed ARDA. The Liberal government was very happy to assume the task of completing and extending that program and making it more efficient.
I was designated as minister responsible for rural development and ARDA. I was glad to accept a new task when the Prime Minister asked me to look after citizenship, immigration and Indian affairs. I was also very happy to see the wise choice made by the Prime Minister when he appointed the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), the member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine, a riding situated in my area, to be responsible for this important task which is called the rural development of a country.
Research and surveys which were essential to efficient and sensible work in the field of rural development pretty soon will 20220-21
The Address-Mr. Tremblay have to give way to important and new achievements for these people who, unfortunately, cannot wait indefinitely for radical solutions to their problems. In many cases, they are already reduced to despair and despondency, wondering whether their voice, weakened after so many years of destitution, will be heard in parliament. Such programs will have to be implemented soon and I trust that the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Made-leine will take the urgent measures which are essential in order to improve the standard of living of these people who are counting a lot on rural development.
Before dealing with the problems which are my special responsibilities as Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, I want to say a few words about the Matane railroad which concerns my own area, the Gaspe peninsula. That question was widely discussed and I feel that explanations are in order, so that the people may know exactly what this is all about.
It is common knowledge that the former Conservative government introduced a bill in the house for the construction of a railroad about 57 miles long, from Ste. Anne des Monts, which would be the continuation of the line between Mont Joli and Matane.
Our opponents used that project as a political football during a few election campaigns, but no one in our district ever felt that it would truly improve local economic conditions. The only thing the people were interested in was the $16 million that was to be spent on the railroad. Everyone was quite willing to let the federal government spend these millions in the district, but nobody could see any use for this railway stretching over a distance of 57 miles, while the terminal point, Matane, is an extremely important town and the real problems in Ste. Anne des Monts and Cap Chat are totally foreign to railroad transportation.
When it came to power, the Liberal government did not divert the funds that had been appropriated for that purpose-because it is very important to note that although the legislation had been passed by both houses, except for a small amount of approximately $50,000, I think, the estimates submitted by the Conservative government never provided any amount for the construction of the proposed railway. This government has preferred to put it aside for the time being, possibly to undertake it later, for who can predict if, in 25 or 30 years, our district will not need a railway. But, for the time being, there are more urgent needs and that is the reason why this government has decided to earmark that amount for useful projects in the area, especially in the transportation and com-

The Address-Mr. Tremblay munication fields, as lor instance, ports, airports, highways, in short projects which come under federal jurisdiction and which will contribute to the prosperity of the area served by this railway.
I was very much surprised when the hon. member for Three Rivers mentioned federal intrusion into the field of education and took exception to the fact that, in the speech from the throne, mention is made of the government's intention, following consultation with the provinces, to introduce a bill concerning student loans. I was also surprised to see that the hon. member who blamed us for applying federal funds to education belonged to the same party as the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Ricard) who has just introduced an amendment to the main motion, asking precisely that federal funds, that is family allowances, be used so that children 16 or 17 years old will remain in school.

speechtext:
The members of the opposition, their leader and his assistant surely need better communication to set up a common policy.
During the few moments I have left, I should like to discuss briefly the department over which I have the honour to preside.
It is well known that the Department of Citizenship and Immigration deals with three main fields:	immigration, citizenship and
Indian affairs, since the head of this department is also the general superintendent of Indian affairs.
I do not wish to refer here to specific measures, as I will have the opportunity to do so either when the estimates of my department are under consideration or when I introduce two bills to be brought before the house, one to amend the citizenship act and the other concerning Indian affairs, more precisely the establishment of a board for Indian grievances.
I shall then have an opportunity to deal with particular policies. But, today, I should like to point out to the house the spirit in which I approach my task in the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
I have a tremendous task, of course, since I follow after my colleague, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), who effected sweeping changes within the Department of Citizenship and Immigration by introducing principles of liberalism which had been missing for so many years. He had to renew the tradition established by a former

minister who had founded that department and had endowed it with a spirit that is still prevailing, but that I am trying to intensify;
I refer to the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill).
What is meant by liberalism in immigration and Indian affairs?
In accordance with the tradition of the Liberal party, that obviously means active sympathy towards the new Canadians who have left their homeland to contribute with the founding groups to the value, to the culture and to the future of our country.
The opening of Canada to immigration means first of all that our new citizens will find an open and friendly welcome upon their arrival here and that they will be treated fairly and charitably. That is what we needed to revitalize our country, as I hope it will be. It means also the active promotion of immigration. In other words, we must not wait for people to come to us; we must go to them by publicizing our country and spreading a true image of Canada abroad.
If we carry out such a liberal immigration policy, there will be much more immigration to help our country prosper. I am not at all worried about the impact that the arrival of thousands of immigrants could have on our country. If, on the one hand, those people come here with a true picture of what our country is like and if, on the other hand, we make a judicious choice of the people we let in, our immigrant population will not feel lost because, while our labour market might not always be in a position to absorb unskilled workers, it can undoubtedly use thousands of trained people.
To be liberal in matters of immigration, that means also to pay particular attention to the new Canadian families who have established themselves and would like to bring their kin over to rebuild, in this country, a family group that may have been broken through years of separation.
It is therefore necessary to make serious propaganda efforts abroad in favour of our country, in view of recruiting the new workers we so greatly need at this time, while protecting the areas where there is a manpower surplus. It also means first to listen sympathetically to the representations of families who want to be reunited, and then to take appropriate measures, legislative measures, if necessary, to enable these families to be reunited and give these Canadians a greater measure of happiness on this land of ours.
I think that Canada's accomplishments as regards the Indian affairs' field are not very impressive. The people from abroad who come

to visit our Indian reserves are disappointed and grieved when they find out the living conditions of many of our Indians in this modern age when educational and cultural facilities are everywhere at a high level but are often non-existent in Indian communities.
Hence, one might say that it is essential -and this is the government's responsibility, that of the Liberal party-to devise as soon as possible a double purpose policy, the first purpose being the encouragement to be given the Indians, that is help them feel more and more proud of belonging to a race as good as any other, by promoting their cultural development in the Indian community itself through schools and the setting up of social groups, which will prompt them to become conscious of the importance of their group and help them maintain their self respect as Indians.
On the other hand, those Indians wish to share the well-being experienced in Canada. They want to work and have their children educated like other Canadians.
Therefore, the federal government must- and that is our responsibility, in co-operation with the provinces, and we shall have a conference in May precisely for that purpose- facilitate, for all the Indians in this country, access to greater social and economic welfare, so that when the centennial of confederation comes, at the time we celebrate the success of our country, the Indians can be proud, not only because they have remained Indians, but because they have succeeded in sharing the same advantages as all other Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, before I conclude, I should like to refer to some particular problems concerning Indian affairs, but I should like to do so in English, precisely in order to show that, in this country, the two official languages must spread as much as possible so that, seeing such comprehension between the founding groups in this country, the new groups which I represent in this house as Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will realize that if there are two official languages and two fundamental cultures in the country, we shall always be glad to give a special place in our community to new Canadians and to Indians who were the first citizens of this country.

When I assumed my new duties I was amazed by the amount and variety of work carried on in Indian affairs and by the importance of the contribution being made to Canada as a whole in this field. There has been an increasing effort on the part of the government to bring the Indians more fully into the economic and social life of our country, and we now see many of our first
20220-21J
The Address-Mr. Tremblay citizens numbered among our best citizens. When I say this, I refer particularly to the Indian leaders I have met in the last few days. I think of Chief Shot Both Sides and some of his councillors from the Blood band, of William Wuttunee, president of the national Indian council of Canada. I have been greatly impressed by the quality and evidence of responsible Indian leadership. I would like to assure you that I have the interest of these people close to my heart and that I shall spare no effort to bring about full equality for them. In order that I may help, as far as I can, to achieve this end, I am determined to learn as much as possible concerning our Canadian Indians, their problems and their aspirations. I shall do this by diligent study and by as many visits to Indian reserves and communities as time permits.
As you know, we are at present seeking the views of the Indians with respect to the provisions of the proposed Indian claims legislation which was introduced last December. We have sent the bill to the band councils^ Indian organizations, Indian friendship centres and many non-Indian organizations as well as the provinces. We have asked for their comments and suggestions. When all the suggestions have been received they will be considered, and it is expected to have the bill, with such changes as may be considered desirable, introduced at a later stage this session. It is hoped that as a result of such legislation, Indian claims which have so long been a source of grievance to Indians can be dealt with in a fair and just manner.
I should now like to turn for a moment to another matter which is assuming increasing importance, and that is the growing efforts that are being made to extend the range of standard provincial services to Indian communities. I believe that we all recognize the need to cut through the wall which has tended to keep Indians separate from the rest of the population. In this regard all levels of government have a vital role to play. I am glad to say that positive steps have been taken in this field. As reported last session by my predecessor in office, the present Minister of Justice, Indian affairs was discussed at the federal-provincial conference in November for the first time. The fact that Indian affairs was on the agenda at all reflects the growing concern about the place of Indians in our country by the federal as well as by all provincial governments. The decision to discuss the matter was in line with the unanimous recommendation of the last joint committee on Indian affairs which examined Indian administration for three years.

The Address-Mr. Tremblay Progress is being made. There is now general agreement that desirable long term objectives for Indian people can best be achieved through the concerted efforts of the federal and provincial governments. It was recognized during the conference that the subject was a most complex one and that it would have to be developed further at later meetings. In fact, I think we can assume that all present at the conference realized that a continuing process of consultation between the federal and provincial authorities and the leaders of the Indian people would be essential to the achievement of the long term objectives. In any event, the conference agreed that discussions on the general subject should be pursued at a further federal-provincial ministerial conference. We are in the process of consulting with the provincial governments concerning the planning of the next conference. We cannot at this time forecast the nature of the discussions that will take place nor the results that will be achieved. However, it is my hope that in the light of the objectives agreed upon in November it will be possible for the next conference to establish basic guide lines for co-ordinating federal and provincial services in policy and program areas. We would hope too that the conference might go even further and establish priority of program areas, such as welfare services, and thus enable federal and provincial officials to work out and develop plans for co-ordinating and implementing these policies and programs.
As I mentioned, the subject of Indian affairs is a most complex one and it is not expected that any single conference or meeting can resolve all the problems that are inherent in improving the welfare of the Indian people. A start must be made at some point, if only on a trial basis, and we hope that the conference will be able to reach agreement in this respect. One of the most difficult tasks confronting us is the development of an effective method of consulting the Indians on the changing pattern in their affairs. We firmly believe they must be consulted and that their co-operation and support are essential to achieving beneficial long range results.
We recognize, however, that it will rarely be possible to achieve complete agreement. As my predecessor stated when the estimates of this department were before the house last December, we must be ready to accommodate ourselves to the legitimate demands of the Indians, and to recognize and respect the different values and aspirations inherent in their culture. We must go much further and create bonds of confidence and mutual respect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first add my words of congratulation to those already extended to the hon. member for Longueuil and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard on moving and seconding the address in reply to His Excellency's speech.
This afternoon I want to take a critical look at the state of the Canada pension plan, said by the Prime Minister in his initial speech to be the most important of all items of legislation which the government will submit this session. In taking a critical look I do not intend to be deterred by the efforts of the Prime Minister, which have seemed to me to be rather clumsy, to make it appear that our party is opposed to a system of contributory pensions in Canada. Following the words of the Prime Minister, as found on page 55 of Hansard of February 20, 1964, to which I have just alluded, the Prime Minister referred to the contributory pension scheme "to which my right hon. friend and his friends are opposed". The Prime Minister knew perfectly well that the words he spoke were wrong. He hopes to silence well deserved criticism of this mess of a plan and to imply thereby that we are opposed to it.
First, all across the country people are wondering about the reason for the rather desperate attitude of the government in trying to jam this piece of legislation through without proper consideration and without proper

consultation and agreement with the provinces. I think the answers are very obvious. All other propositions that the government brought in were washed out in one way or another and they cannot admit that there are errors in this one. Second, they think it necessary that they ride it through before the people know what the plan really is, and this afternoon I hope to point out some of the very serious shortcomings. Third, their hope is that critical analysis will make it appear that we are opposed, which is not the case at all.
To find out what is wrong with the plan we have to find out who is going to lose out if the plan as now proposed is carried into effect. I am going to list six groups of Canadians, constituting 80 per cent or more of our population, who will get no benefit whatever out of the Canada pension plan as it is now proposed. In the first place, the people of Quebec, 5,259,000 according to the 1961 census, will not be included. I will make some remarks about that later.
In the second place, all those Canadians over 65 who are now retired or who will retire before the plan comes into effect will receive nothing out of the Canada pension plan. I think this is something they do not realize but it is a fact that if they are over 65 and have retired there is nothing in the Canada pension plan for them. How many, Mr. Speaker, are eagerly awaiting the implementation of the Canada pension plan in the hope they are going to get something out of it? According to the 1961 census there are 1,084,000 people in Canada outside of Quebec who are over 65. Many of these may still be working and for a fair figure perhaps we should take the number over 70 as a guide, which is 714,674. This group will receive nothing from the Canada pension plan.
In the third place, wives and children of breadwinners need not wait anxiously for the implementation of the Canada pension plan. There is nothing in it for them. There are no survivorship or dependency benefits in the Canada pension plan. It is rather startling to realize that a man could pay into the Canada pension plan all his working years, perhaps for 40 years, and if he died at the age of 64 neither he, nor his widow nor his children would receive one cent from the Canada pension plan. This is a startling provision that I think will cause many to stop and think.
Furthermore, if a person is foolish enough to discontinue a private pension plan with the company for whom he works or even the present civil service pension plans and go into the Canada pension plan, he will find he has gone to a plan which has no survivor benefits from a plan which has. In the event
The Address-Mr. Aiken of his death his widow will discover to her sorrow that only to the extent that the private plan of the former employer provided some benefits, is she going to get anything. This is even worse, Mr. Speaker, when you realize that many people will not understand that there are no survivorship benefits and if they are forced by the method by which the plan is put into effect to discontinue a private plan and come under the Canada pension plan they will be giving up survivorship benefits. I think this should be fully explained because the government cannot give survivorship or dependency benefits without a constitutional amendment, and it was made perfectly clear that they are not going to seek one.
The fourth group who are going to get nothing out of the Canada pension plan are the sick and disabled, the unemployed, the single woman at home, the self employed with very small income and the casual labourer. All need not look for anything out of the Canada pension plan because they will receive nothing. In fact, it is estimated in the government's own literature on this subject that 20 per cent of the male population between 18 and 64 and 70 per cent of the female population in the same age group will not come under the plan. If we look at the figures, according to the 1961 census this means approximately 697,900 males and 2,369,000 females outside the province of Quebec who will not benefit.
In the fifth place, of course, there is a group of 5,888,000 Canadians under 18 years outside the province of Quebec who will benefit very little from the plan. In fact, they will be paying for it all in the next few years. They are the big losers under the Canada pension plan as now set up. The big winners will be the few people who comprise less than 19 per cent of the population of Canada. Young people under 18 will be the losers under this plan because 10, 15 and 20 years from now they will be paying the inflated premiums on the basis of which money will shortly be paid out.
Finally, there are those who have part time employment or seasonal employment or who work for very small wages. They will get very little, if anything, from the plan. All they will get is a pension based on the amount of their wages as reported by their employer or by themselves. I understand it is the intention to make the calculations from income tax returns so, unless there is some other provision, a person who does not file income tax returns will have no way, if he is self employed, of coming under the Canada pension plan. This group will get very little

The Address-Mr. Aiken because they will have accumulated no pension benefits during their working years. I believe this group is the one that most urgently needs assistance under a pension plan.
These are the six identifiable groups of Canadians. I have totalled them up from the figures supplied by the dominion bureau of statistics. There are 14,929,000 Canadians who will not benefit from the Canadian pension plan as it is presently constituted. This amounts to 81.66 per cent of the entire population. There is nothing in it for that group. These are not phony figures. They are taken from the literature that has been supplied by the government and figures obtained through the dominion bureau of statistics census returns that all of us have in our offices, population statistics in Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in addition to those groups I suggest that Canada as a whole will suffer if there is to be one plan for the province of Quebec and one plan for the rest of Canada. This will tend to increase that division that is presently indicated in connection with the problems that we meet here from day to day. Will there not be a very clearly defined line between the province of Quebec and the other provinces if a resident of Quebec benefits in a different manner from the residents of the other provinces? Quebec is striving to evolve a plan of its own. I hope it will be a much better one than this, and probably it will be because Quebec has the constitutional ability to give survivorship benefits which the federal government does not have. Here, you have a distinct division with Quebec separated from the rest of Canada. This does not have to be the case. Arrangements could be worked out so that the two plans will be similar. This is not being done. It is for this reason I say we have to take a more serious look at this whole plan.
I have defined the people who will not benefit under this plan, and I should like now to look at what is wrong with the plan itself, as I see it. First, it encourages inflation by encouraging less saving and more spending. You may ask the reason, and this is it. Those who pay into the Canada pension plan will naturally feel that they are saving for their old age and for their families. Those who pay into the fund will feel that the 1 per cent of their earnings which they pay plus the 1 per cent which is paid by their employers will look after their future. It is well known that in order to be actuarially sound a pension fund requires a payment of at least 5 per cent of the total earnings. This will provide a proper retirement income. Most of the private plans are on this basis. I say that the people having paid this 1 per cent into the fund will
[Mr. Aiken.l

think they have done very well by themselves and their families.
Well, we know that they have done nothing for their families because their families are not included. Furthermore, they should at least be saving the amount of 5 per cent that would be required to give them a retirement income. They will spend what remains of their income after this contribution because that would be the natural inclination. While this may be a good thing in the short run, it is going to drain the savings of the Canadian people and we need this money for investment income. I am going to mention in a few minutes the reason the normal sources of investment income are going to dry up as a result of this plan.
The second real objection to the plan as it is now constituted is that it drains off investment capital from the hands of the public. It will, as I should like to express it, create a stagnant pool of investment funds in the hands of the federal treasury. As first planned, this was to be a "pay as you go" pension plan. In other words, no great sums of money would be built up. But it has now been revised to the point where instead of a $300 million working reserve at the end of ten years we are going to have something like $2.5 billion or $3 billion of working capital at the end of ten years. This is a very large sum of money to be taken out of the hands of private investors and private investment companies. If it were in private hands, it could be used for investment in industrial, commercial or homebuilding enterprises. In the hands of the federal government, it will be dead money, just a debit entry on the books or used by the government in meeting its deficits by the simple expedient of purchasing federal government bonds. I think we can be fairly sure that is what will happen. The amount that has been paid in, then, will be nothing more than a debt of the people of Canada; it will not even exist as live funds. It is for this reason I think the present plan is bad. This money is badly needed in private savings banks for investment and for lending by the banks and by trust companies or insurance companies, but it will be lying dead in the hands of the federal treasury.
I think the provinces have a good case for asking that the bulk of these funds be returned to or used by the provinces from which they came for expansion within the province. It is being suggested now that only 50 per cent be returned to the province. The province of Ontario says we should have 90 per cent of it returned to the province from which the funds came for investment within the province, until such time as the money is needed

for payments to pensions. This sounds reasonable, but it has not been met. I feel that this is another matter that has to be ironed out between the federal government and the provinces.
Surely, the financing of this plan is on the chain letter principle. The principle of the chain letter, as hon. members are aware, is that one letter builds into two, $1 builds into $2, and so forth. Eventually, most chain letter systems break down and someone is a big loser. I am suggesting that the people who are going to be paying into this plan ten or 15 years from now are going to be the big losers. I can see that during the first few years of this plan the money paid in by the working force will be used to pay economic benefits to those who have contributed very little. For example, Mr. Speaker, a person who retires in the first few years of this plan will receive $10 out of the fund for every dollar he has put into it. This sounds rather attractive, especially if you can say you are getting it from the government. However, you are not getting it from the government because the government has not contributed anything.
Where does this money come from? It is going to take ten years, the first ten years, for this plan to build up to even a reasonable equity and another ten years to build the fund to a point where it is going to be run on a proper accounting basis. The money that is going to be paid out in the first ten years will have to come from the future contributors, as I say, the young people and the middle aged people, who will shortly come under the plan. They will be the big losers. They are the ones who are going to have to make up this other $9 that is presently being paid out, and not out of federal funds at all. In spite of the tremendous $2.5 billion or $3 billion reserves that the federal plan will have built up in ten years, it will still be desperately short of money to make the payments as they come due and to carry out the obligations of the plan.
I think there is only one answer. The rate of contributions will have to go up. The government has proposed a palatable plan for the next one, two or three years. It is palatable to those who will go on first, but if the plan is going to pay out $10 for every $1 it receives then something is going to give in future. This is why I call it a chain letter plan, and it will be built up and go flat in the same way as chain letters do.
It cannot be sound on payments of 2 per cent on a person's income because private trusts and insurance companies, and even Canadian government annuities, can only be found sound on the basis of something between 4 per cent and 6 per cent of income.
The Address-Mr. Aiken
Fourth, Mr. Speaker, it will be impossible to tie in any private pension plans with the Canada pension plan. This is one of the things the provinces have been trying to ferret out from the government. How is it going to tie in their private plans, the big plans, the large corporation plans, the civil service plans of both the provinces and the federal government? These plans already in effect are stable, but the Canada pension plan will not be stable.
The amount you get out of the Canada pension plan depends on two or three things. First, it depends on the wages you, as an individual, will get during your working life. How are you going to know, when you start out, how much you are going to be earning 30 or 40 years hence? You cannot be sure, but nevertheless your payments are decided on that basis.
The second thing is the general increase in wages. If you were to go back 20 or 30 years and compare wages then with wages now, and if you had set up a plan on that basis and paid on that basis, it would not have been a very sensible proposal. But this is what is to be done under the Canada pension plan and it is impossible unless there is some criteria, some basis, for saying, "All right, you have got your private plan; you have paid a lot of money into it. You can take that plan and add what you are going to get out of the Canada pension plan and then you will know on what you are going to retire." It will be impossible for the average worker to figure out whether he should drop his private plan with some company or whether he should continue it. This is one thing which has not been settled, and no indication has been given that it will be settled.
Someone may say I am here today fronting for the insurance companies. Mr. Speaker, I do not know any insurance people except the ones to whom I pay my premiums, but we have to look at the figures covering the amount of money held for retirement private plans in Canada, and they are also in the 1961 dominion bureau of statistic's figures.
Trustees-and these are trust plans including private trust funds such as Bell Telephone, the C.N.R., and even public service plans which are all non-profit trust plans held for the employees-totalled 67 per cent, amounting to $4,074,000,000. Some 67 per cent are held in private trusts not connected with insurance companies. Second, the insurance companies hold $1,397,000,000 of trust funds, which is only 23 per cent of the money held in trust for retirement benefits. Canadian government annuities, which amount to $610 million, account for 10 per cent of private

The Address-Mr. Aiken funds. Therefore I am not here to say that private insurance companies are going to lose out, or that their figures should be accepted.
The figures I am giving of 4 per cent to 6 per cent are the average income requirements to make a proper plan, and how the government is going to do it on 2 per cent is absolutely beyond me.
The fifth objection is that the plan creates insurmountable difficulties in the welfare field and uneven distribution of welfare benefits. Those who go on the plan after, say, 10 or 12 years of paying premiums, are going to get an equal amount or even less than those who go on first. This is on an actuarial basis. I do not know why this is done, but this is a fact.
Further, the plan is going to allow the collection of old age security at age 65 on a basis of $51 a month for life. This is an option that is going to be given, according to what we are told. So, who is going to wait until he is 70? Not many people, especially if they can get it without any means test and draw it for life, and in that case lots of people are going to draw it at age 65. But then what happens when they see their neighbour, who retires a year or two later when the plan is in full effect, and he is drawing a maximum of $150 a month? The people who exercised their option at age 65 will say they want more assistance. Where can they get it? They can get it from the old age assistance, and as soon as they start on old age assistance they become an expense to the provinces, including the province of Quebec, because the provinces pay half of old age assistance. This is where they are going to get the extra they need, or else they are going to look to the pension fund, as they now regard the unemployment insurance fund. They are going to say, "There is a nice large fund of $2 billion or $2J billion built up. Why cannot I get some of it?"
It is going to create a lot of dissatisfaction and uneven benefits. One man with small payments will get $150 a month while his next door neighbour draws only $51 a month. The man next door may have been foolish, but there will be no good in telling him that because he will think the government made that offer and that it was practical.
These provisions also create a situation where it is equally or even more beneficial to retire at age 65 than at 70. It is an anomaly in the plan because the rates were revised downwards for those who retire at 70.
My time is about up, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to summarize what I have said and what my feelings are in connection with the plan. First of all, the idea of a retirement plan did not originate with the present government. I think I speak for all in our party 

when I say we are in favour of an equitable retirement pension plan on a scale that the country can afford.
The proposed plan is deficient in that it does not provide survivor benefits; it does not provide equitable coverage; it does not provide an arrangement for the survival of private plans and private capital; and it provides pensions for those who do not really need them while, at the same time, it does not provide the pensions for those who need them most. In fact it subsidizes those who need them least, those in the middle and high income brackets.
Many of the deficiencies can be corrected by consultation, by amendment and by detailed study, but I submit that the effort of the government to jam this thing through, even by putting it to a committee of the house and asking us to sort it out, can never bring about a proper settlement, because the provinces are as fully equal partners in this plan as we are in this house.
