Mr. Speaker, first I want to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. members for Longueuil (Mr. Cote) and Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Basford).
On February 18 we heard the speech from the throne which was read by His Excellency the Governor General. We heard nothing new, for the Liberal party outlined neither its policy with respect to the economy of the country nor the stand the government will take to stem unemployment. In short, they beat around the bush without proposing the required solutions.
Mr. Speaker, If I had to choose the two most important things for our country, I would say that we must first of all find out if we can ensure the country's unity, make it a reality and, if we succeed, to ensure the economic growth which will make of Canada a prosperous country, a happy nation, which will enable it to play a capital role in our rapidly changing world.
Biculturalism and bilingualism, the revision of the constitution, are questions which do not leave us cold. The royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism will, I hope, bring tangible results which will make it possible to amend the constitution so that the two ethnic groups which make up Canada can live in perfect harmony.
I do hope that we shall accept the principle of a complete and perfect understanding between the two great races which built this country. We must never forget that the best agreements were never reached in a lawyer's office or by means of contracts or covenants,

because, fundamentally, any life shared in common is always full of plain, ordinary little things.
I was saying a moment ago that another great problem which interests and concerns us is Canada's economic growth. Whether we like it or not, the present day government is becoming more and more involved in business operations and, through irresponsible actions, may plunge Canada into an economic slump. As a matter of fact, the 11 per cent tax on building materials imposed last summer by the government has had serious repercussions in the field of construction, whatever the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) might think.
If industry increases its production in a general way, it will become important for the government to find a system of fair distribution. It is up to the government to find the means to stimulate this country's economic development. That object will only be attained if the government is able to guarantee a better distribution of manufactured goods. But how can this be achieved? By giving the consumer more buying power. That buying power may be created by reducing taxes or increasing family allowances, or yet by a national dividend.
Those measures would result in an economic upsurge which would create new employment possibilities, to meet the problem of the young people arriving on the labour market.
Mr. Speaker, there is another problem which slows down the rate of economic development, and that is unemployment. A machine which lies idle can deteriorate and its lack of activity means a decrease in production. But the man without a job is deprived of his share in the nation's production and without some needed assistance, he will not be able to feed himself. In our society, nothing is more humiliating and more terrible than forced inaction.
In November 1963, there were 303,000 jobless people registered at the unemployment insurance office. But the most alarming aspect is that forced unemployment mostly strikes at the other end of the social ladder.
Unemployment, that might be called the cancer of Canadian economy, is still too high and has been so for too many years. The government should tackle the problem by resorting not just to half measures, but to spectacular action. The government tried to solve the problem of unemployment by rather conservative legislation, like the winter works program, limited public works, housing aid, etc. Those measures have given some results, but did not have the expected success. It is 20220-22
The Address-Mr. Beaule therefore up to the government to work out complete and permanent measures, even if they entail some risk.
What is needed to make unemployment regress in Canada is, first of all, lower taxes, a vast public works program, municipal loans without interest, as well as the financing of industrial and commercial development, everything being guaranteed by the Bank of Canada.
Through these measures, we would see at one fell swoop unemployment decrease markedly and the rate of economic growth increase more rapidly. The time for action has come and I hope the government will act so as to ensure to millions of Canadians a better economy.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take advantage of this opportunity to state before the house the position of the employees of the Valcartier arsenal, near Quebec city, hundreds of whom live in my constituency.
In November last I asked the following question of the Minister of Industry:
Can the minister inform the house whether he is aware of the situation of the employees of the Valcartier arsenal, and also that materials have been used for purposes other than those of national defence?
The minister answered he was not aware of the situation and would make an inquiry. Two days later he answered the situation was normal. It was at that time I wrote to the Minister of Industry explaining the complaints and the grievances voiced by the employees.
As a result, the minister sent my letter to the president of the arsenals, Mr. J. R. Brisson, and here is the reply I received from the latter:
After conducting an inquiry, I may assure you there are no undue pressures being exerted on our workers at Valcartier. Mr. Simard, as manager of production, is responsible for the efficiency of the department as well as for the delivery of finished products, according to a well-established schedule. As such, he must exercise the controls necessary to achieve this goal. Quotas and cost standards for the production division are established by another department employing industrial engineering methods generally recognized and used in industry.
Those methods take into consideration the employees effort and, far from overloading them, those methods, during the last years, resulted in a great number of changes in our production lines and in a noticeable improvement of working conditions in our plant. Generally, our employees now make a smaller physical effort while attaining higher efficiency.
And here is the inconsistency, Mr. Speaker:
We admit that the employees may be under continuous nervous tension due to job insecurity.
Mr. Speaker, I understand that Mr. Brisson, earlier in his letter, gave the reasons for such working conditions existing in Valcartier

The Address-Mr. Beaule arsenal, but, on the other hand, he realized that the employees were under nervous tension.
I continue:
The considerable decrease in work, personnel reduction and the decision taken during the year to close three plants of the company, contributed to that state of mind.
And as I was not satisfied with the reply, I wrote Mr. Brisson the following letter:
In reply to your letter of December 10, re employees of Valcartier.
The result of your inquiry into the situation of the Valcartier employees does not agree with my own inquiry in this area.
I can assure you that undue pressures are brought to bear on the employees, so much so that they do not know any longer what to do. I also heard that the manager, Mr. Alphonse Simard, uses abusive language with the employees. I learned also that materials were taken outside the arsenal's walls for purposes other than national defence.
I believe that this situation must be remedied immediately and I ask an inquiry by the R.C.M.P. into that state of affairs.
I believe, dear Mr. Brisson, that you will give your close attention to this letter because your answer does not satisfy me.
Mr. Brisson answered as follows on February 5:
In a recent telephone call, I advised you about the steps we had taken following your letter of December 17, 1963.
I can now confirm that following your request, steps have been taken so that the R.C.M.P. may launch an inquiry into the Arsenal Federal de Quebec.
I do not know whether results were obtained, for he merely confirmed that steps were taken. But last Saturday I read like everybody else in the newspapers that the government, through Canadian Arsenals Limited intended to sell the Valcartier workshop to private interests. This proves, Mr. Speaker, that I was right in asking an inquiry in this area.
Today, no doubt because that would hurt someone, rather than making an inquiry, it is merely decided to sell that industry in order to remove every suspicion. Selling the industry will not remove doubts and an inquiry must be made in that area. It was requested many times by the employees. I fully recall that the employees met the present Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) in the 1958 and 1962 election campaigns, when he was candidate in the Quebec East riding, to ask him to intervene with the government to the end that justice be done. But he did not follow up the employees' request. Today, he is in the best position to deal with the government and support the request I make on the employees' behalf.
Therefore, I ask the minister what is the administration costs of the Valcartier arsenals and of the employee classification division, what is the number of foremen and deputy

foremen who do not know what to do but who give orders to the employees, how these orders are passed on to the employees, what is the quantity of materials that was used for purposes other than national defence, a question about which nobody talked because of the blackmailing resorted to by some section heads?
On December 27, the committee which is supposed to represent the employees sent a letter of protest to the minister, asking him not to grant my request and the minister quickly congratulated them. Do you know that that letter was dictated by the section heads and that not a single employee was consulted when the committee took action?
I myself notified the chairman of Canadian Arsenals Limited that the letter, addressed to the minister, did not follow a resolution voted by the employees. On the contrary, that letter was addressed to the minister without the consent of the employees and the chairman of the arsenal was supposed to advise the committee concerned, but nothing was done along that line.
At present, everything is being done to have the employees agree to work 30 minutes more per day, that is two hours and 30 minutes more per week, at a time when in industry, the general trend is to reduce the number of work hours for the employees. In Valcartier, they try to extend working hours, to make the employees work two hours and 30 minutes more per week. People go from one section to the other in the workshop to talk the employees into accepting that compromise, otherwise the workshop will be sold.
You know, Mr. Speaker, that this blackmail system cannot be tolerated any longer and that steps must be taken immediately to set things straight. In the face of such a situation, nothing is said and today, rather than put things in order in that crown corporation, and to guarantee their jobs to all the employees, they prefer to sell the workshop to private interests who, I am sure, will operate with profit.
This all goes to show that there was leakage, patronage and mismanagement. We have every reason to believe that this crown corporation in Valcartier is managed by a group of friends. Rather than accept an investigation which, I am certain, would disclose numerous irregularities, they would rather sell out the workshop.
Mr. Speaker, employees of crown corporations surely deserve to be treated better than that, and the government should do everything possible to guarantee every employee a minimum security through a good and sound administration. Consequently, I ask the minister to do the necessary clean up

so employees can regain confidence and be more efficient. Thus, that crown corporation will be in better shape.
In closing, I ask the minister to step in so that this corporation remains under the ownership of the crown and that arrangements can be made to prevent the sale of Canadian Arsenals Limited in Valcartier.

That this amendment is important is shown by the fact that the principle embodied therein has been adopted by every party in this house, and by at least one provincial government of the same political stripe as my hon. friends opposite. It formed a very major part of the Liberal party platform during the last election and was urged on the hustings by many Liberal speakers who are sitting opposite me tonight.
I should like to draw the attention of hon. members again to page 116 of Hansard for this session. On that page and the subsequent page there is listed some three dozen promises made by the Liberal party during the last election campaign which have not been kept. These were outlined very succinctly by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). I point out that this particular promise is seventeenth on the list. I should like to point out that the extension of family allowances to those in their sixteenth and seventeenth year could well mean, as many hon. members have reason to know, the difference between leaving or remaining at school. The previous government carried on, with considerable success, a campaign to induce young people to remain in school. The basis of that policy was, first, that by remaining in school they improved their capacity later to absorb the skills required for employment in this age of automation. Second, at the same time, they delayed their entry upon the labour market until such time as they were prepared to make a contribution. I am sure that this principle will be selfevident to all members, and that in this year of 1964 it will not be necessary to undertake a campaign to instruct anyone about the value of our young people remaining in school, thereby improving the national educational standards and the opportunities for employment.
The principle contained in this amendment is directed precisely to the age group in which the likelihood of school abandonment is most critical and most disastrous in so far as future years are concerned. Some 300,000 young people in the age group referred to are attending school. A further 300,000 will not continue their education or will start and then drop out unless, through this measure, assistance may be given to enable them to further
The Address-Mr. Winch their education. The passage of this measure would have the effect of assisting a considerable percentage of these young people, some of them among our brightest students, and giving them an opportunity to go on to higher education. I am sure that no hon. member takes lightly the case of the individual student who, having the required capacity, intelligence and desire to learn, is compelled to abandon the opportunity of education on account of lack of funds.
A few minutes ago an hon. member spoke about my experience as minister. I would point out that the most discouraging replies I had to write were concerned with this group of young people, some of them children of widows, who could no longer attend school without some extra compensation. I have had it pointed out to me on more than one occasion that if family allowances were continued, the children could continue in school for a longer period of time, and we all know the resultant advantage of that. I am sure the present minister has had a similar experience, and I am sure all hon. members of the house know of such cases.
Regrettably all too often it is the more deserving students who are affected. Poverty is no respecter of ability. This is a measure, which, if adopted, will have the effect of bringing about that equality of opportunity which is so desirable and which is one of the main objectives of the Conservative party.
When we speak of equality of opportunity, we refer to the application of that principle everywhere in Canada, regardless of race, creed or other discriminating factors. The provision of assistance to young people in school is one important way in which this principle can be applied across Canada without discrimination.
There will be those who, because of political expediency, will be looking for an excuse to oppose this amendment. I repeat what I said about the amendment at the beginning of my remarks; it is a reasoned and reasonable amendment, placed before the house in complete sincerity.
The Prime Minister has said it is time to put partisan considerations aside. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is the opportunity for every member in the house, regardless of party and expediency, to show how this parliament stands on a measure of principle, of benefit to our young people. It is an opportunity for the house to express its opinion on the failure of the government to treat seriously in office what they put forward so loudly and so often when in opposition.

In view of their neglect we all realize, or should realize, that the time is long since passed when there should have been an increase in the age of eligibility and in the rate of family allowances. It is because of the basic recognition of that undeniable fact that the members of this party are going to support both amendments when they are voted on.
Before going into the major section of my remarks, I would like to take the opportunity to make a few brief statements regarding the position of the New Democratic party on certain aspects of government policy. I feel it is absolutely necessary that that should be done, because there is a surprising number of people in Canada who do not recognize that under the procedure of parliament a report of a select, standing committee or a special committee is a majority report. They do not recognize that there is no provision whatever whereby anyone can bring in a minority report to express that he may not agree with some of the aspects of the majority report. As a matter of fact, I would not be very surprised to find that there have been a number of members of the House of Commons who did not recognize that fact.
In order to make the situation clear on certain matters, on behalf of this group I would like to reiterate that the New Democratic party was, is, and will be consistently and continuously unalterably opposed to Canada in any way becoming a "nuclear power, and that we are unalterably opposed to nuclear weapons in Canada and in the hands of our torees anywhere. I also want to say, Mr. Speaker, fEaT~our party supports very strongly all Canadian armed forces for peacekeeping purposes coming under the aegis, and only the aegis of the United Nations.
The New Democratic party also opposes any of our R.C.A.F. squadrons remaining in France under the de Gaulle policy of what is basically military and economic isolation and, because of that country's non-conformity with the nuclear test ban. Also, sir, the New Democratic party opposes what I term the government's stupidity in maintaining army

brigades in Europe on an equipment basis of Honest John rockets which cannot be used in the event of conventional war, unless Canada wants to accept the responsibility of escalating the conventional war into a nuclear war or, in the event of a nuclear attack, having our NATO forces concentrated around Honest John rockets when nuclear strategy is admitted everywhere as calling for dispersal, not concentration.
Whichever way you look at it, government policy as regards our brigades can only be called stupid. It would definitely appear that for some reason or another-unwittingly, if I want to be kind-the policy of the government is that Canadians overseas are expendable. That, we maintain, is an untenable position which can no longer be tolerated and should be corrected as expeditiously as possible.
I shall not deal at greater length now with defence matters, as I understand that in the foreseeable future the government is going to re-appoint the special committee on defence. We also understand that a white paper will be brought down some time in March, so that there will be an opportunity on those two occasions for a full debate on defence matters.
I now want to deal with a subject with which I am very seriously concerned, and it is a most important matter. It is a most serious matter. I refer to homicidally inclined criminals and sex psychopaths who, having been convicted in Canada in the past few years, have returned to acts of violence, to murder and to rape. In order to illustrate the seriousness of the situation which is developing, may I just give a few examples? Take the case of Douglas Brown, committed in the fall of 1961 to Alberta's Ponoka mental hospital because of uncontrollable temper tantrums. He was released in April, 1962. In December, 1962, he moved to Vancouver where he developed a fixation against organized religion, especially against Catholicism. In April, 1963, he took a revolver, went a few blocks down the street and gunned down Father Cuthbert Seward at a Catholic church in my constituency. Thus died one of the finest men I have been privileged to meet and work with-gunned down by a psychopath who had been released as harmless and cured.
Take the case of George Booth who had spent six months in the Essondale mental institution in British Columbia. He was released as harmless and cured. Yet, a matter of days after gaining his freedom he shot to death three R.C.M.P. officers in Kamloops.
Do I need to remind hon. members of the case of Dion, in Quebec, a man who spent most of his life in institutions ranging from

tuberculosis hospitals to orphanages and jails? He was sentenced to life imprisonment and the lash in 1940 for rape. He was released on parole as harmless in 1956 but not long afterwards he was back in prison for committing a homosexual act with a young boy. He was paroled in 18 months as harmless, not dangerous to anybody. Yet, as hon. members know, he confessed to the murder of four young boys.
One more case. In British Columbia we have another sad story. I quote from an editorial which appeared in the Vancouver Province of January 29:
Charles Heathman is a man who has admitted to 54 convictions. He is a man who was twice convicted by separate juries of murdering a ten year old boy and this was quashed by the B.C. court of appeal.
Charles Heathman is a man who was subsequently committed to a mental hospital after he had confessed to a newspaper for $500 that he had killed the Vernon lad.
Now may I quote from an editorial which appeared in the Vancouver Sun of January 28:
Charles Heathman has never been put in safekeeping under terms of the habitual criminal law... As a result of a news story the man was examined by a psychiatrist, declared to be a danger to himself and to others, and committed to Essondale mental hospital.
What happened? This man Heathman spent 20 months in a mental institution. He was then released. He was found to be dangerous by psychiatrists-I emphasize this-only 20 months ago. But on the order of two doctors, neither of whom was a psychiatrist, he was released on the 11th of this month to a sponsor in accordance with the law in Vancouver under strict probationary regulations. Eight days later he disappeared. So, today, this self confessed murderer, admittedly insane 20 months ago, is the subject of a national and international search.
In recent months I have been looking into the situation in the United States and I find a similar problem exists there, only on a far greater scale. I have discussed the situation with constitutional experts and with senior officials of the Department of Justice here in Ottawa and I am told there is no way whatsoever under the Criminal Code by which provision can be made to prevent the release of persons such as I have described in circumstances which would afford greater protection than those outlined in the examples I have given.
I believe it is of the utmost importance that we should do everything possible to protect the rights and privileges of individuals. I say, also, that we have the responsibility of protecting the rights and lives of
The Address-Mr. Winch members of society. Since there is no constitutional power either here in Ottawa or under provincial laws to look after this situation, I should like to recommend to the Minister of Justice and to the government that action be taken at the earliest opportunity to arrange a conference between the Minister of Justice and the attorneys general of the provinces for the purpose of reexamining the provisions of the Criminal Code in conjunction with the provisions of the provincial acts respecting mental hospitals in an endeavour to arrive at a mutual understanding which would prevent the release from mental hospitals of potential killers and rabid sexual psychopaths. Further, I think such a conference should consider the principle that no such persons ought to be released under the authority of general practitioners but only under the authority of psychiatrists, and, possibly, that release not be permitted until there has been further acceptance of the release policy by another psychiatric board.
This is the only solution I can suggest as the best method of handling of this situation. In view of the increasing seriousness of the danger to which citizens are being exposed and in view of the increasing number of occasions upon which prisoners of this type are being released into society, despite their past records of murder and violence, it is my contention that something definite must be done about it at this session of parliament.
I should like to deal, now, with certain problems which arise in the province of British Columbia and, in particular, in the city of Vancouver. It has been my privilege to live in that province and in that city for some 54 years, now, and to have had the honour of being an elected member in that province for 30 of those 54 years. I think, therefore, that I have not only a keen interest in the city and in the province but that I also have a knowledge of its problems and potentialities.
Undoubtedly, Vancouver has one of the finest harbours in the world. It is the third largest city in Canada. It is a major Canadian port and a major port of the north American continent. Yet for some peculiar reason or other it seems to have been completely neglected, as far as development is concerned, not only by this government but by the former government and by the Liberal government before it. And before any action is taken we have to wait until we are faced with situations such as arose a few weeks ago when more than 20 ships were waiting at anchor in the harbour because the port lacked deep sea berths at which they could be loaded and unloaded. Despite the fact that

The Address-Mr. Winch we hear on all sides statements that Vancouver is going to expand rapidly, that its eastern trade is going to expand rapidly, and that the logical port to deal with this increasing trade is Vancouver, we hear of no action being taken to develop the present facilities, and as a representative of Vancouver I say it is high time that this neglect ceased. It is time to stop passing the buck and to state clearly who is responsible. We hear the harbour board saying that development is the responsibility of free enterprise. We hear free enterprise say it is the responsibility of the harbour board or of the government. We cannot pin down who is responsible. I suggest it is time this government found out who has the responsibility and let us know what is going to take place.
If the responsibility to initiate development is on the shoulders of the government, then for heaven's sake let them get down and do something and let the country know what they are going to do. If it is the responsibility of the harbours board, then for heaven's sake the government should tell the harbours board to get moving in Vancouver. They cannot say that they have no money, because I was told only yesterday that the harbours board of Canada has $60 million invested in government funds, and I believe the harbour board of Vancouver has between $12 million to $14 million of that $60 million. That money is there to be used for the development of our harbours, not to get the government out of the sack by investing it in bonds. If the responsibility is upon free enterprise, then let the government tell free enterprise to get off its backside and do something.
In particular, sir, I suggest that the government tell our national railways to do something. At the foot of Main street in Vancouver there is a site owned by the Canadian National Railways in great need of expansion. Why do we not expand it? Are we going to wait for another 20 ships to come into Vancouver harbour? I should certainly like to see the government get after the C.P.R., that Canadian octopus. Let us remember that at the bottom of Granville street in Vancouver we have what is perhaps the finest water site for deep sea shipping in the port of Vancouver. We used to have a deep sea pier there but it burned down in 1938, and the C.P.R. has never rebuilt it. There has been a deep water area there for 35 years but the pier has not been replaced by this company, a company which at times squeals that it does not get enough return from its railway operations. But let it not be forgotten that they received billions out of Canada from land, minerals and other things which were given to them for nothing by Canada.


When we come to British Columbia let us not forget the building of 72 miles of railway on Vancouver island. The Esquimalt and Nanaimo railway owned that 72 miles of railway which was later bought out by the C.P.R., and with it they got two million acres of the finest land on Vancouver Island. In addition, by virtue of chapter 6 of the 1884 statutes of the United Kingdom they not only got those two million acres of land but included with it was coal, coal oil, ores, stones, clay, marble, slate, mines, minerals and substances whatsoever in or under the lands, and also all the foreshore rights in respect of all such lands.
I think, sir, that we have the right to ask this company to do something in the city of Vancouver, to replace that pier which was burned down 35 years ago, and to assist in the development of the major city of British Columbia. They have made hundreds of millions of dollars out of the resources of the people of that province, which were given to them in 1884. I think that is a reasonable request.
Now, sir, there is one other phase which I think is of the utmost importance affecting Vancouver both as a city and as a port, and the province of British Columbia. Canada is a maritime nation. We have thousands and thousands of miles of shore line along the Pacific coast, the maritime coast, Hudson bay and the great lakes. We are a maritime nation, yet the Canada Shipping Act has not had a major revision since 1934. The Canada Shipping Act of 30 years ago is not keeping up with the times. Canadian sailors and Canadian commerce operating around our coastal waters are suffering because of this past neglect. In 1930 and prior years the Canada Shipping Act was, in the majority of cases, concerned with large deep sea vessels or large coastal vessels, but was not concerned with towboats, fishboats and other small commercial-type vessels.
That situation cannot be allowed to continue, because we must recognize that Canada has one of the most treacherous and dangerous coastlines in the world. The coastal waters of Canada are capable of developing some of the most vicious storms known to man. Accompanying the storms are fog, snow, ice, rain, icebergs and rocky coastline. Yet, sir, the Canada Shipping Act is 30 years out of date. Moreover, with modern technology the shipping companies which were previously controlled by both the Canada Shipping Act and the steamship inspection service are now evading the existing laws; because only ships over a certain gross tonnage are governed by the Canadian Shipping Act, which controls where a ship can go, into what waters it can go, how large a crew it has to carry, what

loads it can carry, and the safety measures it should have. In order to escape that control shipowners today-that is, the bad ones, and we have some of them-are building their new ships just a little under the required tonnage and then putting in high-powered engines, so that these smaller ships can more than compete with the bigger, but are not covered by the steamship inspection service or the Canada Shipping Act. As a result there is no control over how many scows or booms they can tow, what loads can be put on the tug itself, how many crew should be carried, or the safety measures which are required. These shipowners escape all this and it is not right.
From talking to those in the know, both sailors and shipowners, I am certain that it is for the sake of the God Almighty dollar, the extra cent, that is the cause, which has resulted, in part at least, in the fact that last year in the Pacific area there were 561 marine distress cases, 29 fishing vessels and towboats sunk, and 25 lives lost. I am pleading with the government to recognize the need for an overhaul of the Canada Shipping Act so as to bring it into line with the needs of today, and to recognize that proper safety requirements and decent working conditions should prevail.
When one speaks of the Canada Shipping Act I think one should also speak of our coastguard service. Canada now has a coastguard and credit should be given to the government for expanding this service. However, Mr. Speaker, I feel it is serving in a negative capacity in that its main function, at least as far as the Pacific coast is concerned, is to be available in case an emergency arises. It is our belief, sir, that it can be given a positive role, apart from just being available when an emergency arises, by functioning as an inspection team to go out into the waterways of the Pacific, of the Atlantic and of the great lakes, and under an up to date Canada Shipping Act inspect the vessels on the waterways to see that they meet all the requirements of safety and proper working conditions. Not only would that make for a better coastguard service, but also, if properly handled, it would, I am convinced, save a considerable amount of money for the taxpayers of Canada. We now have this peculiar situation: the Canadian coastguard is comprised of ships and boats of the Canadian steamship inspection department, the Department of Fisheries, the marine biological department, the hydrographic surveys department, weatherships, lighthouse tenders, Department of National Defence vessels, and so forth, each of which is operating on its own. Not only that, sir, but when a civil servant
The Address-Mr. Matheson of one department has to go to a certain area he cannot get on any boat except the boat of his department, even if the boat of another department is going there, it is the most stupid thing I ever heard. Surely a co-ordination of these services would enable them to do this specific, detailed work of the department to which they are connected or the particular type of work on which they have been instructed. Under a co-ordinated plan of a coastguard service, whereby all the officers and men of these ships know the regulations, the safety rules and the steamship inspection services, they could do a better job in our coastal waters to bring about greater safety and thereby greater efficiency.
I do hope that the government will take this matter under advisement, Mr. Speaker, and will take action this session with regard to some of the problems which I have had the privilege of drawing to your attention. May I, in conclusion, say that we are here as elected members with a responsible job, and as far as the New Democratic party is concerned we will look at all measures on the basis of need, constructiveness and principle and will then judge our position accordingly.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was born in Quebec, raised and educated in Quebec, worked in Quebec until the exigencies of war service took me abroad. For 23 years my father served as a minister of one of the old historic congregations of Quebec city. In speaking on the subject of Quebec and its place in the unity of Canada I speak of my home-my native land, my special country- I will not use the word state. Quebec is part of the true north strong and free which in the words of O'Canada I have for so long pledged myself to defend.

Mr. Speaker, may I say boldly and unequivocally that there are many millions of Canadians who stand prepared to defend this land, this land that runs from sea to sea, against any enemy that may threaten from without or from within. Our feet were set in a large room and what affects the Columbia watershed, or Bell island or Rouyn, Quebec, or any Canadian person anywhere affects me too; and as the member for Leeds where begins the noblest river that runs to ocean, I intend to say my piece.

Because it was my fortune to be bred a Quebecker I speak on this subject of national unity not out of anger but out of love.

The Address-Mr. Matheson

In the language of Shakespeare, Canada is going through the winter of our discontent. It has been said that Quebec is now undergoing an almost convulsive effort in the fields of education, industrial development and selfawareness. When we look to biblical authority, the gospel of St. Mark gives us this advice:
And if a kingdom be divided against itself-
This applies to the kingdom of Canada:
-that kingdom cannot stand.

And a house divided against itself falleth. [Text]
Many hundreds of years ago a sermon was preached by a man in St. Paul's cathedral in the days when William Shakespeare was acting on the stage. The preacher was John Donne, and he said:
No man is an Hand, intire of itselfe; every man is a peece of the Continent, a part of the maine; if a Clod bee washed away by the Sea, Europe is the lesse, as well as if a Promontorie were, as well as if a Mannor of thy friends or of thine owne were; any man's death diminishes me, because I am involved in Mankinde; And therefore never send to know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee.
Yet when I look at our newspaper at home, The Recorder and Times of Brockville of February 1, 1964, I read:
"That's the ultimatum", said party leader Real Caouette at a press conference following the rally.
"If we don't get that, it's definite. Bang, it's all over, we get out of confederation".
What does he ask for? He asks for absolute control over the creation of credit for Quebec, control over its imports and exports, absolute control over immigration, the return to the provinces of direct and indirect fiscal resources.
In my upbringing as a boy I remember, je me souviens, the first motto I was taught, and of course what each of us remembers of our heritage is different.

And I remember the terrible day in 1940 when France fell. It was a day of shock and horror and utter sadness. I have the most vivid recollection of separating myself from my fellow soldiers in order that I might weep alone. And the fortunes of western civilization might well have been destroyed had England been unable to withstand the fierce onslaught which followed-the turning point in history which we now refer to as the Battle of Britain. This too is part of our memory. Our own Leonard Brockington refers to our Canadian casualties in these words:
[Mr. Matbeson.l

He said:
Upon these pages are inscribed the names of those gallant Canadian airmen who fighting in the stricken skies of Britain died to defend and save a sanctuary of our ancestral freedom. Their motherland remembering her young sons rejoices that such men once lived and will forever grieve that they died so young.
Bom of the sun they travelled a short while toward the sun and left the vivid air signed with their honour.
My friends, among those who left the air signed with their honour was Canada's fighter pilot Camille Robespierre Bon Seigneur of 257 squadron, R.A.F., shot down on September 3, 1940, and Pilot Officer Alex Albert Gray Trueman of 253 squadron, who was shot down in flames the following day. What would these two think of a divided Canada?
I remember vividly the costly and abortive raid on Dieppe which occurred on August 19, 1942. The lessons learned in this Canadian blood bath paved the way for the successes of D-Day more than two years later. I was at first divisional headquarters at that time, receiving the earliest intelligence communications and listening to those dreadful reports as they came in. I will never forget that day. Let me tell the house of just one little incident.
I learned these facts from a devoted friend of mine, Reverend Dr. Waldo Smith, M.C., of Queen's theological college, who is something of a military historian. Among the prisoners taken by the Germans at Dieppe were elements of Les Fusiliers Mont-Royal. German intelligence officers were clever enough, and knew enough about Canada and about the difficulties we were experiencing with our different ethnic backgrounds in this country that they tried to play up one group of prisoners against another. I am told that prisoner of war parcels were distributed and the Germans gave generous chocolate rations to Les Fusiliers. These men, were hungry and utterly weary, and ready to devour it like hungry wolves until they noticed that no chocolate was available to their English speaking comrades. The chocolate was returned and no more was accepted by Les Fusiliers until there was equity among all our men. What would those veterans who loved one another more than themselves think of fracturing and separating Canada? I must say I like my friend, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), but I don't like what I read in the Brockville Recorder and Times of February 1, 1964, when he said:
-Canada's economic regime "will be reformed in an orderly fashion, or there are some people who will destroy it in disorder and blood". Wartime conscription was carried out "in the name of liberty, in the name of Christianity", he said.

"We've got to steal your children from you-that's what was done during the war, ladies and gentlemen. And now people blame our youths."
The news story was headed: "They Stole Arms; Gov't Stole Sons for Butchery in War, Says Caouette".
A few days ago I was in Washington and I saw that moving play by John Hersey, "The Wall", which is a story of what happened in the Warsaw ghetto under our modern Christendom just a very short while ago, a story of how in one city alone 500,000 Jews were killed in the most brutal fashion possible. One of the lines in this play runs this way:
I used to think what was important was just to live; then I learned that what really mattered was how and with whom.
I want to tell my friends, even those who take a very different view from mine on the matter of separatism, that we feel very strongly about unity and the business of actually living with them. For my part I cannot conceive of this country in any other form or structure than a Canada consisting also of the French people.

One of the crowning satisfactions of my life has been that I had the honour to serve for many months as a forward observation officer to the celebrated Royal 22nd Regiment in Sicily and Italy. Indeed throughout the Mediterranean campaign. I wore their hat badge alongside my own gunner badge.
Let me tell you about this regiment, because among the first division men, this regiment was legendary and incredible. Always before battle we knelt for prayer-and the padre prayed in this wise:
Make us brave God and resolute to do our duty. And may we so conduct ourselves this day that we will give solemn pride to all Canadians."

Over 20 years have passed but I cannot forget these impressions. I cannot think of Quebec in any other way than with that gallant French Canadian padre on his knees bringing us together before battle. It was a pretty hard thing, I want to tell you, to try to march with the Royal 22nd Regiment because it was always a question of whether you could master your fear enough to meet the standards of that brave company. Happily some of their great ones are alive today, our Vanier, our Bernatchez, our Triquet, our Turcot.

But there are silent ones who cannot speak. What would they say about some of the shameful speeches made this and last month in the St. Denis and Laurier by-elections about Canada dragging young men out of cellars to serve their country.
The Address-Mr. Matheson
Let me just give you the names of a few of my dead comrades whose deeds are more eloquent than words. These men came from the cities and the remote places. I have seen many of their plain white crosses.

Incidentally that same padre friend of mine, Waldo Smith told me a few days ago that he has done some research on the battlefields of Sicily and Italy and he tells me that the number of French Canadian names that we had in our regiments in the Mediterranean that had nothing to do with the French Canadian regiments far exceeded in numbers those that were in the four historic French Canadian regiments. They served in the artillery, the service corps, the provost corps. Everywhere we had these French comrades.

Listen to these names: Corporal Villeneuve, Lieutenant Chicoine, Private Arsenault, Sergeant Bouillon, Private Levesque, Private Pelletier, Corporal Santerre, Private Tarte, Private Desrosiers, Private Godin, Sergeant Legare, Corporal Gagnon.
Let these 12 stand as a guard of honour for those who cannot speak.
These French Canadians, my brothers, who have given everything they had, everything they hoped they could have been, must have a say in this business too. How would they feel about a divided Canada?
My father died not many months ago and before he died he told me something I was glad to hear and I was glad he told me what he did. He said that during the war years it was a moving experience for him to arise early in the morning and to watch the commandant of M.D. 5 passing the manse at 67 Ste. Ursule with his lady on his way to early morning service in the winter, and I might tell you that walking through the snowdrifts in Quebec city on a wooden leg was not easy and would not be easy even for a young hockey player. This great gentleman, Vanier, was walking there to church in spite of his disability that resulted from his service in the first world war.
Eugene Forsey has put it this way:
. Canada is both two nations and one, two nations in the ethnic, cultural, sociological sense-
Thank God that is so in a world like ours. We certainly need the wider vision that we could not possibly have with one narrow strain.
-but one nation in the political, legal, constitutional sense.
And presiding as the Queen's representative over this one nation is this gallant and godly gentleman who is beloved by all Canada.

The Address-Mr. Matheson
Terror is not a new weapon. Not long before his death the late President Kennedy remarked that throughout history it has been used by those who could not prevail either by persuasion or example. He went on to say that inevitably they fail, either because men are not afraid to die for a life worth living or because the terrorists themselves come to realize that free men cannot be frightened by threats and that aggression will meet its own response.
A few days ago I was in Quebec city and I went to see the Wolfe monument. We have all read about what happened there and I am sure everybody has mixed feelings on the matter. I remember years ago hearing rather insulting comments passed between different ethnic groups in the British army. If you were Scottish you told the story one way. If you were Irish you told the story another way. The story goes that you send in the Scots in the first assault, then you send in the Irish to kill the wounded and then you send in the English to rob the dead. Of course, if you were English you told the story with a different sequence. But surely there is nothing less worthy than this business of pulling down a monument at night, a monument to a man who died for his country over 200 years ago in following what he felt was his path of duty. Surely we as parliamentarians, without pointing scorn or contempt at anybody, have got to uplift our national ideals and standards to the point that this will be made clear. I want to say that I would be shocked and hurt to think that there would be any English speaking Canadian who would dare do anything to dishonour, for instance, the monuments to Dollard des Ormeaux or the Marquis de Montcalm or the great missionaries like Jean de Brebeuf and Gabriel Lalemant. Do French Canadians think they own these men? They are a part of Canada and surely even James Wolfe is a part of Canada too.
I notice that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) is looking my way. Having said what I have about monuments I also say that maybe it is time the historic section of the minister's department started to take a close look at the inscriptions because some of these inscriptions are far less than gracious and appropriate to this present day. I should like to give an example. I see the distinguished Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in his seat. He and a number of others in this house belong to the national trust of Scotland. I know that a good number of them contributed to a monument at Culloden. My ancestors were defeated at Culloden. They were Scottish Presbyterian Jacobites who were fighting for

a French prince and were proud of him. They looked upon him as their sovereign.
They believed that Charles was their sovereign. That defeat is the reason they reluctantly left that country. It is the reason they became, if you like, royalists over here. In any event, there was no shame about that event at Culloden. There was great pride in having risked all. The battle of the plains of Abraham affected the history of our country. These are things that are common property. They are precious and very important to all of us.

Let us start anew, reminding both sides that politeness is not a sign of weakness.

Politeness means communication. A few days ago when I was in Montreal I heard a story about the Ontario miner who felt that English was the only language we needed. After all, was it not the language used by Jesus in the sermon on the mount? This is what he thought. Then, there is the little story about the meaning of the term "bilingual". You say a person is bilingual if he can speak English and French. If he is trilingual, he can speak one other language in addition to English and French. However, if he is unilingual, he is "maudite Anglais". Senator Pouliot has said he suspects the farmers of Ste. Modeste are not going to learn to speak English, nor does he believe there is much hope the farmers of the Okanagan valley are going to learn to speak French. I am inclined to agree with him. I believe this is true of many other of our people.
However, what a wonderful objective it would be for the country if many of us with Anglo-Saxon backgrounds were to urge our sons and their sons to take some of their education in Quebec or, if you like, even in France. We have three young, vigorous members of the cabinet who are French, one of whom was educated at Cambridge, one at Oxford and one of whom graduated with his doctoral degree from the University of London.
Senator Power has said that perhaps what we need is more honest fist-fights. I recall that I always got licked by a French boy every day on the way to school and I got licked by an Irish boy on the way home from school. During recess there was always a battle between the English and the Scotch.
Then, too, I recall that one of the delightful and memorable events of my youth was a Sunday School picnic to the sugar bush. It was the season for that event, and we had about 15 or 18 boys. Having had enough maple sugar, we felt it was a good time to

take on the French boys and we did. We damaged each other as much as possible for about two hours, then came home and got our lickings from our parents. I still look upon those events as very fine lessons in race relations. If I may use the language of Arthur Miller I would say, "Silence is not going to solve it any more". We have had too much silence.
According to the language of the Psalmist He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the rivers unto the ends of the earth. Surely, it follows that where the King of Kings has dominion, in this country, all men are brothers.

These times for Canada are climacteric and difficult but I do not believe that any of us, French or English, would exchange places with any other people or any other generation.

I like the words of that great play, Henry the Fifth. Eric Christmas gave me these lines where Shakespeare is speaking about the romance between Harry of England and Princess Catherine of France, "God, the best maker of all marriages, combine your hearts in one, your realms in one". Let us emphasize the importance in this country of learning, after a great many experiences which were bitter and difficult, that we have a rich ethnic heritage which can now mean so much. Today we talk about a tunnel between England and France, and we talk about the north Atlantic community comprising North America and Europe. I marvel at the wonderful position we enjoy if we will only take advantage of this rich heritage of English and French, of common and civil law, of Protestantism and Roman Catholicism, all moving together in the direction of bringing this troubled world into some kind of order.
If I may end with the language of Laurier, he said this and his words sum it up better than anything I could hope to say:
Faith is greater than doubt and love is stronger than hate.
